Szeroko zakrojone plany miały w okresie dwudziestolecia międzywojennego wynieść Zamość do roli ważnego wielofunkcyjnego ośrodka w centralnej Polsce. Konieczna była likwidacja zapóźnienia gospodarczego względem innych części kraju, uwarunkowanego czynnikami społeczno-gospodarczymi, militarnymi i politycznymi. W tym celu dążono do zainwestowania w miasto i region zamojski. Wykorzystując centralne położenie Zamościa zaplanowano tu duży węzeł komunikacyjny, opierający się na magistralach kolejowych północ–południe między Gdańskiem a Odessą oraz Lwowem a Zatoką Fińską, a także wschód–zachód między Zagłębiem a Wołyniem. Przez region przebiegać miała autostrada A1 łącząca Gdańsk i Gdynię ze Lwowem i portami czarnomorskimi oraz ważna arteria z Zagłębia Świętokrzyskiego przez Sandomierz, Włodzimierz do Kijowa. Plany reformujące strukturę administracyjną kraju zakładały przekształcenie Zamościa w ośrodek wojewódzki, natomiast projekt Centralnego Okręgu Przemysłowego uczynić miał z Zamojszczyzny rejon aprowizacyjny COP z dominacją przemysłu spożywczego i lekkiego. Planów tych nie udało się zrealizować z powodu wybuchu II wojny światowej871. W międzywojniu Zamość liczył się jako ośrodek oddziałujący pod względem gospodarczym, kulturalnym i usługowym na okoliczne powiaty składające się na region Zamojszczyzny, tj. zamojski, tomaszowski, biłgorajski, hrubieszowski i krasnostawski. Znajdowały się tu instytucje o znaczeniu ponadpowiatowym, m.in. sąd okręgowy z prokuraturą, instytucje administracyjne oraz oświatowe. W strukturze przestrzennej Zamościa usytuowane centralnie Stare Miasto obejmowało 530 ha oraz 230 w zdecydowanej większości murowanych budynków. W 1919 roku zamieszkiwało tam około 8 tys. osób, wśród których było 5574 Żydów i 3 prawosławnych. Liczba stałych mieszkańców zmniejszała się na skutek rozbudowy przedmieść. W 1935 roku na Starym Mieście zameldowanych było 7620 osób872, natomiast przed wybuchem II wojny światowej – 4858 osób. W 1939 roku na Starym Mieście oraz przy kilku sąsiednich ulicach mieszkało łącznie 6141 osób873. W obrębie staromiejskich bloków zabudowy powstało kilka nowych budynków, m.in. modernistyczna kamienica czynszowa Stanisława Czerskiego przy ul. Przybyszewskiego 18 oraz kamienica czynszowa Lipczyńskich przy ul. Pereca 6. W otoczeniu Starego Miasta nie udało się wybudować dużej dzielnicy urzędniczej zaplanowanej na Plantach w 1922 roku oraz kameralnego osiedla dla pracowników kolei według projektu z 1920 roku, które miało wyrosnąć na terenie folwarku wojskowego na Podgroblu, a które przed II wojną światową zaczęto wznosić na Karolówce874.

Dążąc do przywrócenia pierwotnego wyglądu Rynku Wielkiego, stopniowo powycinano drzewa z jego powierzchni oraz usunięto drewnianą zabudowę i studnię875. Na skwerach urzą- 871 Ibidem, s. 105. 872 APZ, AmZ (jak przyp. 617), 1580–1952, sygn. 200. 873 APZ, AmZ (jak przyp. 617), 1580–1952, sygn. 641, s. 16–19, 874 J. Żygawski, Niezrealizowane projekty śródmieścia Zamościa w XIX i XX wieku na podstawie archiwalnych opracowań kartograficznych i planistycznych, „Teka Komisji Urbanistyki i Architektury PAN Oddział w Krakowie” 43 (2015), s. 140–141. 875 APZ, AmZ (jak przyp. 617), 1580–1952, sygn. 595, s. 1, 25. dzono trawniki i klomby kwiatowe, zlikwidowano w 1938 roku skwer przed ratuszem. Wzorem innych miast Rynek Wielki przemianowano na plac Adama Mickiewicza, chociaż w 1939 roku rozważano powrót do dawnej nazwy. W trakcie podjętych w latach 1936–1939 prac konserwatorskich przeprowadzono renowację placu rynkowego, w drugiej połowie lat 30. odremontowano kamienice oraz gmach ratusza przywracając mu barokowy wygląd. Działania te wykonano pod nadzorem dr. inż. Jana Zachwatowicza z Politechniki Warszawskiej, konserwatora wojewódzkiego Józefa Dutkiewicza, architekta miejskiego Tadeusza Zaremby i starosty Mariana Sochańskiego876. Natomiast Rynek Solny nadal pełnił funkcję głównego ośrodka handlowo-usługowego Starego Miasta. Jego przestrzeń zajmowały stragany i rzędy kiosków, z których sprzedawano różne towary oraz artykuły spożywcze. W podcieniach kamienic działały sklepy i składy oraz punkty usługowe. Utrzymano rekreacyjny charakter Rynku Wodnego, urządzając tam zadrzewiony skwer z alejkami. W 1920 roku kolegiata jako pierwsza budowla w Zamościu uzyskała status zabytku877. W 1929 roku rozpoczęto przebudowę sygnaturki i dzwonnicy. Remont kościoła przeprowadzono w latach 1937–1938. Prace ograniczyły się do pomalowania wnętrza oraz odnowienia ścian zewnętrznych878. Podczas II wojny światowej Niemcy zamknęli kościół w 1940 roku, urządzając w nim punkt zborny dla wysiedleńców z Wielkopolski. W latach 1941–1944 obiekt zamieniono na magazyn żywności. Od 1918 roku trwały starania o przekazanie gmachu dawnego kościoła Franciszkanów prowincjałowi zakonnemu. Mimo przychylności władz wojskowych oraz administracji diecezjalnej odbudowa i rekoncyliacja kościoła okazała się nieopłacalna. Wojsko przekazało budowlę w 1921 roku władzom miejskim, które ulokowały w niej Sejmikowy Dom Ludowy, siedzibę Sejmiku Powiatowego, Powiatową Kasę Komunalną, kinoteatr „Stylowy” oraz muzeum879. Po likwidacji Teatru Miejskiego gmach kościoła reformackiego przekazano Kościołowi katolickiemu na potrzeby duszpasterstwa szkolnego880. Rekoncyliowano go 4 września 1927 roku jako rektoralny kościół pw. św. Katarzyny881; podczas okupacji niemieckiej pełnił funkcję parafii, przeniesionej z kolegiaty. W zabudowaniach poklaryskowskich umieszczono siedzibę policji oraz Ochronki św. Franciszka. Na górnej kondygnacji dawnego kościoła pw. św. Anny powstała sala widowiskowa882. Dawną cerkiew bazyliańską okupacyjne władze austriackie przekazały w 1915 roku Kościołowi katolickiemu, 20 października 1918 roku rekoncyliowano ją jako kościół szkolny pw. św. Stanisława Kostki. Usunięto cebulastą kopułę latarni nad jej nawą oraz latarnię z kopułką nad prezbiterium. Na polecenie biskupa lubelskiego 4 sierpnia 1934 roku kościół przejęli redemptoryści. W 1941 roku Niemcy przekazali

876 Odnowienie Rynku zamojskiego w świetle prawdy. Wyciąg z protokołu Nr 57 Rady Miejskiej m. Zamościa w dniu 4 lutego 1939 r. w sali Rady Miejskiej w Ratuszu, „Teka Zamojska” 1–3 (1939), s. 46–50. 877 S. Misieczko-Rudnik, Prace konserwatorskie w Zamościu w latach 878 J. Kowalczyk, Kolegiata (jak przyp. 217), s. 43; S. Misieczko-Rud- 879 E. Lorentz, Kościół i klasztor (jak przyp. 689), s. 26, 28. 880 A. Kędziora, Dawna architektura (jak przyp. 275), s. 36. 881 S. Misieczko-Rudnik, Prace konserwatorskie (jak przyp. 877), s. 32. 882 A. Kędziora, Dawna architektura (jak przyp. 275), s. 37. świątynię prawosławnym. Obiekt ponownie rekoncyliowano 21 stycznia 1945 roku jako kościół pw. św. Mikołaja. Poprawiono infrastrukturę w sferze ochrony zdrowia, uruchamiając w 1928 roku przy ul. Lubelskiej 1, w sąsiedztwie Parku Miejskiego, Stację Opieki nad Matką i Małym Dzieckiem (tzw. Kropla Mleka) będącą ośrodkiem zdrowia z poradniami specjalistycznymi883. W tym samym roku uruchomiono w dworku przy ul. Lwowskiej 14 nowoczesne Kąpielisko Miejskie884. Przy silnej konkurencji między hotelami „Centralnym” i „Victorią”, w zaadaptowanym budynku Bramy Szczebrzeskiej otwarto w 1924 roku Sejmikowy Dom Noclegowy, w 1935 roku przemianowany na Hotel „Sejmikowy”. W okresie II wojny światowej Niemcy urządzili hotel w klasztorze Redemptorystów oraz zamknęli w 1941 roku hotele „Centralny” i „Victoria”, zamieniając ich pomieszczenia na kwatery prywatne; jedynie część jednego z nich wydzielono jako „Hotel Central”, który działał do sierpnia 1944 roku. W czasie I wojny światowej uruchomiono Elektrownię Miejską, na jej potrzeby adaptowano pomieszczenia podwalni oraz Bramy Lwowskiej Nowej. W 1919 roku dobudowano maszynownię, doprowadzono bocznicę kolejową oraz rozebrano dwie kazamaty podwalni od strony północnej. Ograniczone możliwości lokalowe sprawiły, że w latach 1924–1926 wzniesiono przy ul. Sienkiewicza 22 nowy budynek elektrowni. W 1930 roku przedsiębiorstwo zaliczane do największych pracodawców w Zamościu przekształcono w Okręgową Elektrownię Miejską, doprowadzającą prąd m.in. do Izbicy, Komarowa, łabuń i Zawady885. Do większych zakładów zaliczała się Spółdzielnia Mleczarska Powiatu Zamojskiego, przeniesiona w 1930 roku z Janowic Małych do budynku dawnej łaźni wojskowej przy Rynku Solnym. Przed wybuchem II wojny światowej unowocześniony zakład miał zapewniać aprowizację Centralnego Okręgu Przemysłowego. Od 1921 roku w oficynie północnej dawnego pałacu Zamoyskich działała Drukarnia Sejmikowa, natomiast na placu przy Bramie Lwowskiej Nowej – Betoniarnia Sejmikowa, relokowana w 1939 roku na Podgroble886.

Na przedmieściach działały niewielkie zakłady produkcyjne: młyny, olejarnie, wytwórnie wód gazowanych, rozlewnie piwa, piekarnie, masarnie, tartaki, fabryczki narzędzi rolniczych, szczotek oraz gilz do papierosów. Na terenach pofortecznych za Bramą Lwowską Nową, między ul. Lwowską a linią kolejową, na działkach dzierżawionych przez przedsiębiorstwa związane z obsługą rolnictwa, m.in. Bank Ziemiański, Spółdzielnię Rolniczo-Handlową „Snop” i Lubelski Syndykat Rolniczy, powstały różne bazy i składy. Największym tego typu zakładem było działające w latach 1918–1926 Towarzystwo Akcyjne „Ziemianin” z kompleksem budynków obejmującym m.in. duży młyn i kaszarnię. W 1931 roku przeniosła swoją siedzibę ze Zwie- rzyńca do Zamościa firma Polski Przemysł Drzewny „Czerski & Jakimowicz”. W jej skład wchodziły dwie fabryki: Mebli Giętych w Bondyrzu i Sklejki we Lwowie-Kozielnikach oraz tartak w Zamościu na Przedmieściu Lubelskim887. Właściciele chcieli w śródmieściu wybudować nową siedzibę firmy, zamiar udaremniła wojna. Firma Polski Przemysł Drzewny „Czerski & Jakimowicz” planowała zainwestować w budowę fabryki mebli w Zamościu. Gdy w 1932 roku magistrat rozparcelował grunty miejskie położone między ul. Sienkiewicza, terenem nowej Elektrowni Miejskiej, ul. Kolejową, linią kolejową do Hrubieszowa oraz gruntami Popówki888, firma zakupiła siedem działek, na których zamierzała wystawić budynek fabryczny z kominem oraz domy mieszkalne. W przyszłości planowała także korzystać z bocznicy kolejowej doprowadzonej do Elektrowni Miejskiej oraz deklarowała partycypowanie w kosztach konserwacji toru889. Ostatecznie inwestycja nie doczekała się realizacji. W sferze projektów pozostała również organizacja Zamojskiego Okręgu Przemysłowego dla 7 powiatów, stanowiąca zaplecze COP. Od końca lat 30. trwały także intensywne przygotowania do budowy w Zamościu zakładów fermentacyjnych Monopolu Tytoniowego oraz filii Fabryki Artykułów Elektrotechnicznych inż. Stefan Ciszewski i Spółka w Bydgoszczy. Ich sfinalizowanie uniemożliwił wybuch II wojny światowej. W sieci komunikacyjnej Zamościa najważniejsza była tranzytowa droga z Lublina do Lwowa, stanowiąca odcinek drogi państwowej nr 8 z Gdańska przez Warszawę, Lublin, Lwów do Okopów Świętej Trójcy i dalej w kierunku Odessy oraz Istambułu. W latach 30. planowano przekształcić ją w autostradę stanowiącą transeuropejski korytarz transportowy oraz główny ciąg komunikacyjny kraju w relacji północ–południe890. W dwudziestoleciu międzywojennym wytyczono kilkadziesiąt ulic w obrębie dzielnic oraz zmodernizowano kilkanaście ulic, m.in. Akademicką, Sienkiewicza, Zamkową. Planowano wybudowanie kilku obwodnic pozwalających ominąć m.in. Stare Miasto oraz Zamość na trasie tranzytowej między Lublinem a Lwowem i Szczebrzeszynem a Hrubieszowem. Zorganizowano dworzec autobusowy zapewniający skomunikowanie Zamościa m.in. z Lublinem, Lwowem, Warszawą, Biłgorajem, Tomaszowem, Chełmem i łodzią.

W czasach II wojny światowej Niemcy zamknęli w Zamościu wiele budynków lub zreorganizowali działalność na zasadzie sukcesji funkcji. Do wielu obiektów cywilnych wprowadzono funkcję przemysłowo-składową. W bożnicy staromiejskiej ulokowano stajnię, następnie dużą stolarnię, których funkcjonowa- 887 J. Wojciechowska-Kucięba, Zagraniczna korespondencja handlowa firmy „Polski Przemysł Drzewny – Czerski i Jakimowicz”, „Archiwariusz Zamojski” 7 (2008), s. 47. 888 Obecnie kwartał położony między ulicami: Sienkiewicza, Pod- 883 R. Ostrowski, Gospodarka miejska w Zamościu, Zamość 1929, 885 R. Ostrowski, Gospodarka miejska (jak przyp. 883), s. 33. 886 APZ, AmZ (jak przyp. 617), 1580–1952, sygn. 202, s. 28; ibidem, sygn. 204, s. 1, s. 67; Studium historyczno-urbanistyczne przedmieść (jak przyp. 702), s. 136. 890 Droga miała omijać Zamość od północnego wschodu obwodnicą. Trasę obwodową uwzględnili w projekcie planu zagospodarowania przestrzennego Zamościa z 1939 r. Jan Zachwatowicz oraz Władysław Wieczorkiewicz. J. Żygawski, Sieć dróg w Polsce. Program budowy autostrad, Lublin 2002, mps w Bibliotece Wydziału Nauk o Ziemi Uniwersytetu Marii Curie-Skłodowskiej w Lublinie, s. 44. nie przyczyniło się do dewastacji obiektu. W 1941 roku zamknięto dla wiernych kolegiatę lokując w jej wnętrzu magazyn zboża oraz składnicę sprzętów. Obiekty poforteczne pełniły funkcje magazynów, garaży i składnic wojskowych891. Zmieniono nazwy wielu ulic i placów w mieście. W ramach programu „Otto”, stanowiącego przygotowania do ataku na ZSRR, Niemcy zmodernizowali w 1940 roku infrastrukturę kolejową. Rozbudowano część techniczną stacji Zamość o kilkanaście dodatkowych torów oraz ładownię Nowa Osada. W 1942 roku wybudowano na stacji murowaną parowozownię z budynkiem administracyjnym oraz budynki zarządu drogowego przy ul. Szczebrzeskiej. Po II wojnie światowej nastąpiły zmiany struktury społeczno-własnościowej w centrum. Zasiedlano staromiejskie kamienice pożydowskie, a przy tym zaniedbywano budynki pod względem komunalnym i konserwatorskim, co dało negatywny wizerunek Starego Miasta. W wyniku przeprowadzonych prac renowacyjnych i konserwatorskich w latach 70. oraz po 2005 roku sukcesywnie zmniejszano udział powierzchni mieszkalnej na rzecz usług. Nie udało się w pełni usunąć lokali komunalnych zdominowanych przez mieszkańców z pogranicza marginesu społecznego. W 1996 roku Stare Miasto zamieszkiwały 1754 osoby. W trzydziestoleciu powojennym Zamość rozwijał się zgodnie z założeniami gospodarki socjalistycznej jako stolica regionu Zamojszczyzny, będąca centrum administracyjnym, usługowym i gospodarczym dla okolicznych powiatów. Sterowane centralnie inwestycje objęły przede wszystkim przemysł, który zapewniał okolicznej ludności pracę i koncentrował się w zaprojektowanej jeszcze w latach międzywojennych dzielnicy przemysłowo-składowej położonej we wschodniej części miasta, wzdłuż linii kolejowej do Hrubieszowa. Po 1950 roku ulokowano tam m.in. duże zakłady mięsne, chłodnię, elewator, kombinat budowlany, fabrykę mebli, spółdzielnię mleczarską, fabrykę domów, liczne bazy i przetwórnie. Wzrost liczby mieszkańców znalazł przełożenie w inwestycjach budowlanych. Powstawały nowe osiedla – zarówno zabudowy jednorodzinnej: Podgroble, Zamczysko, Promyk, Wiśniowa, Karolówka, Powiatowa, jak i zabudowy wielorodzinnej: Ludowego Wojska Polskiego, Planty, Orzeszkowej. W ramach planowania rozwoju gospodarczego kraju w latach 60. pojawiły się projekty urbanistyczne rozwoju śródmieścia oraz wschodnich dzielnic mieszkaniowych: „Centrum Usług Ogólnomiejskich”, „Dzielnica Wschód” oraz „Nowy Zamość”, które miały związek z planami podniesienia Zamościa do rangi miasta wojewódzkiego oraz jego uprzemysłowienia. Wiele z zaprojektowanych wówczas założeń komunikacyjnych zrealizowano w kolejnych dekadach892. W 1974 roku włączono do Zamościa wieś Sitaniec-Błonie, przekazując do gminy Zamość część nieużytków.

Po wojnie Stare Miasto wymagało ogromnych nakładów finansowych z powodu tragicznego stanu większości kwartałów zabudowy. W 1957 roku zmodernizowano kwartały zieleni na pl. Mickiewicza, urządzając klomby, alejki i miejsca wypoczynku. Plac Mickiewicza stał się obok Parku Miejskiego najpopularniejszym miejscem wypoczynku mieszkańców Zamościa oraz coraz 891 A. Kędziora, Dawna architektura (jak przyp. 275), s. 33, 39, 43, 892 J. Żygawski, Niezrealizowane projekty (jak przyp. 874), s. 142–146; B. Nowak, J. Żygawski, Zamość. Ulice (jak przyp. 9), s. 107–108. większej rzeszy turystów893. Rynek Solny utracił status centrum handlowego na rzecz Nowego Rynku oraz targowiska miejskiego przy ul. Bazyliańskiej. Postępowała degradacja Rynku Wodnego jako placu publicznego. W latach 60. rozpoczęto pierwsze po wojnie prace renowacyjne w obrębie Starego Miasta. Odnowiono wówczas m.in. gmach „Podkarpia” oraz wschodnie bloki zabudowy. W gmachu poklaryskowskim mieściła się siedziba komendy Milicji Obywatelskiej, następnie dom dziecka. Rozbudowywano bazę turystyczną, która opierała się krótko na hotelach „Centralnym” i „Staromiejskim” (Brama Szczebrzeska) oraz domu wycieczkowym PTTK (dawny kahał). W latach 1967–1971 wybudowano przy ul. Greckiej 6 nowoczesny hotel „Renesans”, który kontrowersyjnie wpisał się w krajobraz Starego Miasta z powodu posadowienia na fundamentach świątyni ormiańskiej894. W arsenale umieszczono bazy i składy, stolarnię oraz hale montażowe zakładów produkcyjnych895. Teren baz i składów za Bramą Lwowską Nową przy ul. Partyzantów przejął Państwowy Związek Gminnych Spółdzielni „Samopomoc Chłopska”. W 1960 roku dworzec autobusowy relokowano z pl. Wolności na plac przed Bramą Lubelską Nową. Na początku lat 70. rozebrano kilka bocznic kolejowych w rejonie Starego Miasta. Na mocy ustawy z 28 maja 1975 roku896 wprowadzono dwustopniowy podział administracyjny kraju, w wyniku którego Zamość został podniesiony do rangi miasta wojewódzkiego. W 1974 roku Zamość otrzymał centralne fundusze na zaplanowaną na lata 1975–1985 rewitalizację Starego Miasta. Za czasów „wojewódzkich” miał nastąpić dynamiczny rozwój miasta. Zakładano powiększenie jego obszaru do ponad 54 km2 oraz wzrost liczby mieszkańców do 100–120 tysięcy w 2000 roku. Ze względu na kryzys polityczno-gospodarczy miasto rozwijało się jednak wolniej niż pierwotnie zakładano. W zakresie inwestycji mieszkaniowych oraz rozwoju przestrzennego odnotowywano znaczący postęp. Powstały osiedla zabudowy wielorodzinnej: Orzeszkowej, Kilińskiego, Wiejska, Słoneczny Stok oraz zespół trzech osiedli „Nowe Miasto” ze wzorcową w kraju jednostką osiedlową „PR-5” (program rządowy nr 5), a także kameralne osiedla rozrzucone w różnych częściach miasta. Kontynuowano zabudowę jednorodzinną w obrębie osiedli: Karolówka, Rataja, Nowe Miasto i Janowice Duże. W 1989 roku uchwalono podział Zamościa na osiedla mieszkaniowe, likwidując tradycyjny podział na dzielnice (zniesiono m.in. Przedmieście Lubelskie, Podtopole i Janowice Małe). Zmodernizowano sieć komunikacyjną miasta tworząc arterie dwujezdniowe oraz budując dwie śródmiejskie obwodnice897.

Po 1989 roku rozwinęła się baza noclegowa w Zamościu. Na Starym Mieście działa 7 hoteli, kilka pensjonatów oraz kilkanaście kwater turystycznych. Kilka hoteli powstało w obrębie innych osiedli. W 1975 roku przeniesiono ze Starego Miasta na Nowe Miasto dworzec autobusowy. Pod koniec lat 70. zamierzano zlikwidować średnicową linię kolejową przebiegającą przez centrum i wyprowadzić tor na północną obwodnicę kolejową przy Linii Hutniczo-Siarkowej (LHS)898. Nadrzędnym celem była rewitalizacja Starego Miasta w obrysie dziewiętnastowiecznych fortyfikacji. Dążenia te nasiliły się po 1992 roku, kiedy wpisano Stare Miasto na Listę Światowego Dziedzictwa Kultury UNESCO. Na zmiany nie godziły się władze kolejowe, gdyż linia przecinająca centrum stanowiła ważny element komunikacji dalekobieżnej. Po 2000 roku zaznaczył się regres połączeń kolejowych z Zamościa, zaczęto zamykać infrastrukturę przewozową. W 2009 roku zawieszono połączenia kolejowe; przywrócono je od marca 2011 roku. Zmodernizowano linię średnicową budując dwa przystanki kolejowe oraz stację towarową.

Zamość was founded in the central part of Zamość Basin, known as Zamość Vale (Padół Zamojski)1. This mesoregion represents the southern part of Lublin Upland, and is bordered by Giełczew Uplant and Grabowiec Divides from the north, by Roztocz and western edge of Sokal Ridge from the south, and Hrubieszów Basin from the east2. This 870-square-kilometre Zamość Vale is a latitudinally oriented concave formation, a hundred kilometres long and a dozen kilometres wide, with a relief deposited during the Quaternary. The subsoil of its flat, occasionally waterlogged terrain consists of Upper Cretaceous marls and chalk3, with quite diverse soils: loessal brown soils, chalky rendzinas, podzols on sands and, over large parts of wide river valleys, fertile fluvisols4. The surface of the Vale has been chiselled by the waters of the Wieprz River and its tributaries5. One of them is the łabuńka, which was called Kalinowica in the Middle Ages and early modern times. At the city’s future location, this river joins the Topornica, then called Wieprzec6. The morphology of its former name indicates that it was a deminutive of the name Wieprz; it was used to refer to the whole stream of the river up to its confluence with the Wieprz, also after its confluence with Kalinowica. Accordingly, Jan Zamoyski adopted the name for the city he was founding, announcing in the incorporation document that it would be called “Zamoście nad Wieprzcem”, and the site he selected is located below the point where the Kalinowica flows into the Wieprzec River. 1 M. The valleys of these rivers are wide, sometimes their reach is only limited by the edges of the hills surrounding Zamość Vale. Prominent features of the landscape are the extensive floodplain terraces, also known as humps, rising up to 40–50 m above the river valleys, formed out of marls, more impervious to water damage than chalk. Their slopes are generally long, gently sloping, often with extensive downslopes in the lower part. Between such humps, drainless depressions, floodplains and peat bogs were often formed7.

At the foot of one of these humps, on a loessal supra-valley terrace located on the right bank of the łabuńka River, at an altitude of ca. 215 metres above sea level, Zamość, i.e. a town “within walls”, was founded. Its suburbs were delineated and built up to the east, north and west of the terrace. On the southern side, in a very marshy area, the łabuńka River flowed into the Topornica River. Their waters, joined in a single channel, flowed from the west around the elevation chosen for the foundation of the town and then headed towards the Wieprz River. At that time, the junction of the two rivers was near Żdanów. After the causeway was built in 1582–1585, a “Great Lagoon” was created to the west – “ku Płoskiemu” – into which their waters flowed. To the north, beyond the first causeway, a “side” causeway was built across the Wieprzec River, which connected the Lubelskie Suburb (Przedmieście Lubelskie, from Lublin, a city eighty kilometres northwest from Zamość) with the area beyond the Wieprzec River, and in front of it, the “Little Lagoon” was developed8. The extensive hydrographic network around the town required constant restoration and drainage works, both in the 17th and 18th c.9 It was not until the beginning of the 19th c., with the significant decrease of water level in the Great Lagoon and the transformation of the Little Lagoon into a marshy meadow, that new channels of both rivers were dug, diverting the łabuńka into the southern city moat10. 7 H. Kędziora, Zalew Wielki i Mały (as n. 8), p. 784. The vegetation of the Zamość area is rich and varied. Already in prehistory and the Middle Ages, as a result of human activity, forest complexes were almost completely wiped out. The small oak, hornbeam, pine, fir and spruce forests found here originated either as a result of planting or in a natural way. The surrounding area abounds in scrub11. The fauna of Zamość Vale, also rich and varied, has undergone major changes over the centuries due to human activity12. The climate of the area has been influenced by a continental climate, characterised by cold winters and hot summers. Until recently, these seasons lasted 90 days each, while the others lasted 60 days each. The plant growing season was about 214 days long. Precipitation levels were among the relatively high ones, amounting to about 600 millimetres per year. Some climatic peculiarities observed in the mesoregion are the result of the relief – its concavity in relation to the surroundings. Incoming air masses cannot easily escape the basin, resulting in lower temperatures in winter and higher temperatures in summer, as compared to the neighbouring areas of Lublin Upland and Roztocze. Zamość land has the lowest level of evaporation of water from the surface in Lublin Upland, the lowest degree of cloudiness and some of the highest values of insolation13. The oldest traces of human habitation in the area of the future town and neighbouring villages date back to the Late Palaeolithic period (12000–7900 BC)14. They were discovered at a multicultural site in the village of Sitaniec-Wolica. They included flint tools: a Lyngby-type leaf-shaped blade and two microlithic scrapers attributed to the Świder culture (8800–8300 BC)15. With further warming of the climate, another period in history began, called the Middle Stone Age or Mesolithic (7900– 5500 BC). The communities of the time transformed their economy, making it easier to obtain food and lead a more sedentary lifestyle, mainly in river valleys, associated with gathering, hunting and fishing. Settlements were then established on sandy and dune areas. Remains of Mesolithic encampments are known from the villages of Wólka Wieprzecka and Topornica16.

Around the middle of the 6th millennium BC, the first groups of newcomers from the south arrived here, bringing along the ability to rear animals, grow crops, produce improved stone tools, and make and fire clay pots. Neolithic settlement (5500– 2200 BC) ushered in a sedentary lifestyle and the construction of permanent settlements, traces of which, as well as their cemeteries, remain in the area of our concern. These newcomers included representatives of the following cultures: Linear Pottery (5500–5200 BC), Lublin–Wołyń (4700–3400 BC), Funnelbeaker (4200–2900 BC), Globular Amphora (3500–2700 BC) and Corded Ware (2900–2200 BC). Remains of these groups were encountered in Hyży, łapiguz, Mokre, Pniówek, SitaniecBłonie and Wolica, Szopinek and Żdanów17. In the Zamość area, a grave of the Globular Amphora culture was discovered near the Church of St. Michael in the Lubelskie Suburb; its equipment included two flint axes and a fragment of the bottom part of a clay amphora18. Two stone axes were found in the Old Town – one near the New Lubelska Gate (Nowa Brama Lubelska), the other in an unknown location19. Around 2200 BC, new civilisational ideas began to arrive in the area, associated with the use of copper and tin alloy, i.e. bronze. The Early Bronze Age (2200–1600 BC) is represented by artefacts found in Kalinowice, Hyza, łapiguz, Pniówek, Sitaniec-Kolonia and Wolica, Szopinek and Żdanów, left by the people of the Mierzanowicka (2200–1600 BC ) and Strzyżowska (1750–1600 BC) cultures. In the 16th c. B.C., the people of the Trzciniec culture (1600–1200 B.C.) appeared here with characteristic burial mounds. Traces of their residence were found in Hyży, Pniówek, Sitaniec-Błonie, Szopinek and Żdanów20. In the funerary rites of this culture we observe the occurrence of biritualism, leading to the spread of corpse-burning in the Lusatian culture. The finds confirm the strong links between the two cultures21.

The Lusatian culture (1200–400 BC), coinciding with the end of the Bronze Age and the early Iron Age, dominated settlement in Central Europe. The area on the Wieprz River belonged to its eastern range22. It was already common for people of this culture to use bronze products, later also iron, and their livelihood was based on agriculture. They burned their dead on funeral piles, collected the burnt remains in clay vessels called cinerary vessels buried them in cemeteries established on hill slopes or near rivers. Rarely, they buried them directly in the ground (pit graves). These cemeteries, but also related ceramics, were discovered in Kalinowice, Mokre, Pniówek, SitaniecBłonie, Wolica and Szopinek23. The period of Roman influences is characterised by intensive mobility of peoples of various cultures. In the 2nd c. CE settlers of the Wielbark culture (3rd–4th c. CE), identified with the Goths, arrived here; their traces in the form of pottery were discovered in Sitaniec-Błonie26. This period has left a number of coin finds and metal artefacts. Many traces of the residence of peoples of various cultures have survived from the period of the migration of peoples (5th and 6th c. CE); however, the mobility of these groups caused the territory on the Wieprz River to become deserted28.

In the second half of the 5th and in the 6th c., Slavs gradually arrived in the territory of the Zamość land. This was followed by a period of settlement stabilisation, which lasted at least until the middle of the 10th c. The inhabitants of the emerging settlements are classified as members of the Lędziany tribe, belonging to a large community which was formed at the time in the basin of the Vistula and Odra rivers29. The process of constant densification of the settlement network is confirmed by archaeological finds dated back to the early medieval period, recorded in the area of all villages adjacent to the territory of the future town. However, they are dated quite widely, from the 6th to the 13th c.30, therefore, can hardly be used to establish the ethnic changes in 24 Ibidem, p. 99, 139. However, they confirm, at least until the beginning of the 11th c., the affiliation of the inhabitants of these settlements to the Western Slavic branch, i.e. to the Polish state31. In 981, the area was claimed by Kievan Rus. In the archaeological material from the 11th–13th c. from Czermno (Czerwień) and Sąsiadka (Sutiejska), as well as from other sites, East Slavic artefacts – the so-called Ruthenian pottery – appear, indicating a change in the ethnic composition of the settlement, although contacts with Lesser Poland and Masovia are also confirmed32. This was the consequence of the change of state affiliation and the acquisition of these territories by Kievan Rus in 103133 The actions of the Kievan state were followed by the consolidation of the Polish-Ruthenian state border near the Wieprz River and the absorption of most of the former Lędzian tribe by the East Slavic groups34. The area we are interested in ended up on the eastern side of the border. The new political affiliation was followed by ethnolinguistic, religious and cultural changes resulting from the adoption of Byzantine rite Christianity by Ruthenia. Therefore, the region became an area of the Orthodox Church activity and became part of its territorial structures, which reinforced these changes35.

Further development of the areas on the Wieprz and łabuńka rivers took place within the framework of territorial structures known as wołości, i.e. gord districts, the centres of which were located in Czerwień and Sutiejsk36, and, after their disappearance in the 13th c., within the gord districts with centres in Szczebrzeszyn and Grabowiec37. A settlement network of a given district was associated with these strongholds, becoming increasingly sparse as one moved away towards the periphery38. The peasants were settled on farms, which might be called manors. They formed a village managed by an official called a ciwun (tywun). Their duties were rendered in natural resources (grain, honey, hides) and unpaid labour39. Villages on the Wieprz River and its right-bank tributaries, located at the border of the Sutiejski (Szczebrzeski) and czerwieński (later Grabowiecki) districts, were rare. From the end of the 14th c., these settlements were mentioned in written sources. In the period of the disintegration of Kievan Rus (after 1054), for more than two hundred years the territories on the Wieprzec River changed hands several times, belonging to various district principalities, in which the authority of the princes was not very stable, hardly contributing to economic and social development41. The situation of the inhabitants was also adversely affected by the external situation and the continuous invasions into the Duchy of Halych-Vlodzimiersk by its neighbours in the 13th c.: Lithuanians, Yotvingians, Poles and Hungarians, as well as three Mongol invasions42. The situation on the border with Lesser Poland was, therefore, constantly uneasy and tense, even in the next half-century, although the political rapprochement of Prince George II with the Piast kings of Poland, Ladislaus the Elbow-high and Casimir the Great, promoted mutual contacts between the inhabitants of villages and towns on both sides of the border, and even migration43. The cooperation of Halych-Vlodzimiersk Prince George II with Poland provoked opposition from the magnates in his state; they formed a conspiracy and in early April 1340 the monarch was poisoned in Volodymyr44. The state was plunged into a decades-long crisis, and the Poles (supported by the Hungarians), Lithuanians and Tartars began to compete for its territory. The areas of our concern on the Wieprzec and Kalinowica rivers came under the rule of the Polish king as a result of the Polish-Lithuanian treaty of 1366. In the Duchy of Belz and Chełm, the power was maintained by the Lithuanian Duke George Narymuntowicz, who initially was a vassal of Casimir the Great. After the death of the Polish king in 1370, George Narymuntowicz broke the feudal ties and incorporated the lands of the Duchy into the Lithuanian state45. Seven years later, after the expedition by Louis I of Hungary, King of Poland at that time, they were taken back. Prince Władysław Opolczyk ruled there for a short time, and in 1378 the whole territory of Red Ruthenia was taken under the Hungarian administration. It did not last long, as around 1379 the Szczebrzeski district was granted by King Louis I of Hungary to the Crown Treasurer Dymitr of Goraya, and from then on it formed a private estate46. Her marriage to Duke Jagiello resulted in the Polish-Lithuanian Union. It was of crucial importance for the development of the entire territory between the Vistula and Bug rivers, including the south-eastern edge of the Szczebrzeskie district, which encompassed villages on the Wieprzec and Kalinowica rivers. The Polish-Lithuanian Union, during the period of modernisation and development under the Jagiellon kings, contributed to the elimination of the atmosphere of unrest and menace throughout the borderlands. It also provided the conditions for economic and social development47. Existing villages began to be remodelled for new settlers from Poland, who were allocated land under German law. The lands allocated to peasants were measured in units called lans. A three-field system was introduced, whereas peasants’ duties were reformed, replacing in-kind payments and forced labour with monetary rent. Elements of self-government were introduced in the form of a village council headed by a village leader, called sołtys. As a result of these changes, villages were settled by a mixed Polish-Ruthenian community48. Colonisation and the structural transformation of settlements laid the foundations for the development of a market economy. The processes of modernisation of the villages on the Wieprzec and Kalinowica rivers began in the second half of the 14th c., but information concerning them only comes from later times. The first mentions of these villages occur in written sources from the end of the century. In 1398, Kisielów (Hyża), Mokre, Płoskie and Żdanów were mentioned; in the latter, a parish church was recorded in 1424. In 1404 Pniów (Pniówek) was mentioned, whereas in 1423 – Kalinowice49. In 1450, Skokówka, also known as Skokowice, was recorded in the sources, which, according to Kazimierz Sochaniewicz, “had previously formed a single topographical and organisational unit with the village of Żdanów”50. All these villages belonged to the Szczebrzeskie estates and were granted by their owners as fiefs to the nobility associated with them51. Janiowice, adjacent to Skokówka from the north and first mentioned in 1417, belonged to the Grabowiec district in the Belz Duchy of Siemowit IV52. To the north of it there was a village of Sitaniec, in the Krasnostawski district of Chełm Land, mentioned in 1402, in which before 1434 the owner, Wojciech Sitański, founded the Parish Church of St. Bartholomew53. The parish included Szepin (Szopinek) mentioned in 1450, which was part of Grabowiec district54.

In the late Middle Ages, Skokówka Castle and the surrounding villages belonged to the Szczebrzeszyn district, which had been transformed into a private property. They were located on its eastern border and, together with it, were part of the Krasnostawski court district of Chełm land. The owners of Szczebrzeszyn and the district exercised jurisdiction over these villages under feudal law67. The Zamoyskis, having acquired Skokówka and the neighbouring settlements in 1517, obtained an exemption from feudal dependence68, thereby making their estates judicially free from the authority of Szczebrzeszyn. Until the first partition of Poland in 1772, they were fully connected with the Krasnostaw district69. The boundaries of the town of Zamość, apart from the lands of the villages of Skokówka and Kalinowice, also included the village of Janiowice, which belonged to the Grabowiec district of the Belz voivodeship70. At the beginning of 1580, Jan Zamoyski made efforts to buy this village from Piotr Janiowski; the purchase was completed the following year71. The foundation of the city was initiated by Jan Zamoyski (1542–1605), an eminent man, statesman, promoter of science and culture, well-known in early modern Europe81. He owed his rapid career to his close cooperation with King Stephen Báthory. The construction of the residence had probably been planned by the chancellor for some time. It was to consolidate his ascendancy, satisfy his ambitions and serve for propaganda purposes83. For this investment, he chose a site in the estate acquired by his grandfather Feliks on the Wieprzec and Kalinowica rivers, near the Skokówka castle. This place was to recall the traditions of Zamoyskis – Jelitczyks, whose memory was propagated by the chancellor84. During the long stay of the royal court in Lviv, from 14 May to 10 September 157885, the chancellor met the already well-known Italian architect, Bernard Morando from Padua, who was employed for the construction work. Zamoyski chose him as the main contractor for the planned project. In Lviv they probably had plenty of time to discuss plans for the construction of the residence, and on 1 July Zamoyski concluded a contract with Moranda for the “masonry”. The contract referred to the erection of a castle, but there is no doubt that the chancellor was considering the simultaneous foundation of a town associated with it, which would be an economic base for the residence and the centre of the owner’s surrounding estates86. Such a foundation model was then widely used in the organization of new towns87. On his way back to Cracow from Lviv, the chancellor went to the Skokówka estate and stayed there until 2 October88. It is probably then that he chose one of the hills in Żdanów for the site of the planned castle89, positioning the structure in the centre of his estate, near the road from Szczebrzeszyn through łabunie Małoniż to Belz90. At the same time, he made efforts to buy the village of Mokre, situated to the north-west of Żdanów, from Zofia Niedźwiecka, which he acquired for 4700 zlotys. For this purchase he obtained the consent of the owner of the Szczebrzerzyn estate, Andrzej Górka, who also freed the chancellor from the feudal dependence imposed on the village91. Zamoyski intended to connect the city to these buildings and surround the entire complex with a moat and fortifications. Therefore, the chancellor planned to build a modern fortress. The quoted fragment of the document’s disposition constituted the programme of the investment. The second part of the disposition contains the main rules for the organisation and functioning of the municipal commune, which, by the will of the founder, was to be autonomous and self-governing. The chancellor, therefore, announced the appointment of a competent locator of the town, i.e. the vogt, who would be familiar with urban problems and the organisation of trade. He recommended that the prospective citizens of Zamość should engage in crafts and trade, and not cultivate the land, the task he deemed more suitable for villagers. He promised to endow the citizens with plots of land, with fields and meadows of half or a quarter lan each. This was intended to make it easier for the citizens to obtain food.

Zamoyski proclaimed that he wanted “there to be only one Roman Catholic faith in this city”, allowing only Catholics to settle. Describing the citizens’ obligations, he freed them from peasants’ and serfs’ services and dues, corvées, labour service and elements of ius ducale (Polish: podwoda, the obligation to provide horse carriage). He also granted the citizens an exemption from paying rents for twenty-five years. After this period, the plot owners were to pay annually, on St. Martin’s Day (11 November), 6 grosze from a house in the city to the city lord and additional 3 grosze to the church; in the suburbs, 4 grosze to the city lord, 2 grosze to the church; from each half-lan, 20 grosze to the city lord, 6 grosze to the church; from a quarter-lan, 10 grosze to the city lord, 3 grosze to the church. The functioning of the urban municipality was to be based on the provisions of the Magdeburg law, “which is used by royal towns”. All citizens and residents of the city and suburbs were to be under the single jurisdiction of the city authorities; the issuer of the document relinquished, also on behalf of his successors, the judicial power over the citizens of Zamość. They were to be tried exclusively by the court presided over by vogt and lay judges, which was to issue verdicts. The burghers could appeal against them not to the lord’s court, but to the court of appeal of the German law in Lviv. The structure of the urban government was to be similar to that of other towns under German law: it was to be made up of a mayor, a bench of lay judges and a town council. The city founder intended to appoint the first officials in these offices, and later the citizens themselves would “elect and appoint” them. The election of the authorities was to take place in the presence of “the hereditary lord, or their delegate”, to whom the elected would be sworn. The oath was also to be taken by the elders of the craft guilds, the existence of which was provided for in the charter. The charter issuer also promised to establish a procedure for settling disputes between the citizens and the city lord, and declared that the charter would be improved in the future and that changes would be confirmed with the king. Furthermore, the chancellor promised to send the document to the royal court within eight weeks and to ask the king for per-

Permission was also needed to allow the citizens to hold weekly markets on Wednesdays, and fairs three times a year: on the sixth Sunday after Easter (between 4 May and 6 June), on St. Mark’s Day (7 October) and on the Feast of the Conversion of St. Paul (25 January). Zamoyski also declared that for Zamość citizens he would seek an exemption from state taxes for a certain period of time, a perpetual exemption from customs duties on the territory of Poland, and an exemption from border customs duties for “a certain amount of time and certain amount of money”. In addition, he announced that he would be sending a request to the king for a privilege to store salt and other goods. As announced, the chancellor sent his document to the royal court in Vilnius. Stephen Báthory signed two diplomas on 12 June 1580. The first contained a confirmation of the charter, giving it public status101, the other was the proper royal charter, drawn up in accordance with the form for this type of deed102. The king agreed to the city’s incorporation, bestowed Magdeburg municipal law, excluded the city’s territory from the reach of Polish law, freed its inhabitants from the jurisdiction of regional officials, and confirmed the weekly market and the calendar of fairs, which were to be modelled on those in Lublin and Toruń. He also granted a partial staple, ordering merchants visiting Zamość to present their goods, “transported to central Poland from Volhynia, Belz Voivodship and Chelm Land, and other goods transported in the opposite direction, also from Gdansk”, for three days. The king announced that from then on privileged roads to Volhynia and Lviv would lead through Zamość. Upon royal decision, a customs chamber and a salt storehouse were placed in Zamość. The monarch exempted Zamość citizens from paying taxes to the Commonwealth for a period of fifteen years, from paying customs duty in the entire country indefinitely, and once they had paid the great and border customs duty, the Crown Treasury was to refund Zamość citizens 300 zlotys annually for ten years. The city was also granted a coat of arms, depicting St. Thomas the Apostle with a spear. All three documents formed the basis for the legal incorporation of the city of Zamość, which only gained full status as a municipal centre on 12 June 1580, in accordance with the legal order of the Commonwealth and the monarch’s incorporation regalia.

Following the recommendations of Italian urban planning literature, the castle was based on a quadrilateral plan and the town on a hexagonal plan104. It seems that the designer was too optimistic in assuming the possibility of enlarging the chosen elevation from the south and north, so that the shape of the hexagon adopted for the city would be symmetrical in relation to the centreline, linking it to the castle, and so that eight bastions could be built, as in the view of Zamość in the sixth volume of Civitates orbis terrarum105. Only in the following years did this prove impossible. Hence, Morando changed the location of the quadrangle of city space, moving it slightly to the south and west, and bringing about the necessary compromise of the project with the terrain conditions106. The main axis of symmetry, linking the city to the castle, was refracted at its entrance gate or at the marketplace that was created between the castle ramparts and the city area107. As a result, the spatial layout of Zamość was based on an asymmetrical hexagon108. In the complex of the residence and the city, the chief place was given to the castle, the main centre of lord’s power over the surrounding estates and, from 1589, over the Zamoyski family entail (Polish: Ordynacja Zamojska). The residence was to consist of the main palace, called the “front” or “grand” palace, and two “rear tenement houses”, i.e. a palace for the founder’s wife and an outbuilding. The structure was later surrounded by defensive and decorative fortifications: A quadrangle of walls with two corner bastions and an axially positioned gate, enclosing an extensive courtyard. The castle gate was an important element in the composition of the entire layout, being a common point for the axis of the castle and the city. An arsenal was planned to be built near the castle109.

The residence was separated from the city by an extensive elongated marketplace, which Jerzy Kowalczyk called a place of concentration of spiritual and intellectual life, and Teresa Zarębska called a “weapons ground”110. To the south, it ended at the planned church, situated, as the old tradition goes, between the residence and the city centre, while to the north a school was to be located, later to become the Academy111. The civic quadrangle, on which the axis of the castle’s connection with the city continued, was delineated on a rectangular plan. According to Adam Miłobędzki’s findings, the western part of Hrubieszowska Street, which emerged from the Salt Market, was not given a name, while the last street, Szewska, continued through the entire layout of the city116. Miłobędzki, who reconstructed the network of streets and the parcelling of blocks many years ago, revealed that when designing the entire city Morando used a large (measured in rope units) and small (measured in perch units) surveying grid, which he also applied when dividing the urban space into streets, squares and blocks, and that the location of the palace and the temple referred to it. In his measurements, the architect used a rope 45.467 m long and a perch 4.5467 m long, as well as an elbow measuring 60.6 cm117. Between the streets and squares he delineated rectangular blocks of plots. Miłobędzki distinguished three groups of blocks:

a. The first group consists of blocks with a single row of generally narrow plots; in the city nearly half of the blocks belonged to this group. They occurred in strips, comprising the northern and southern market blocks and their extensions towards the west, as well as the blocks in the northern frontage of Szewska Street. The market blocks were wider than the neighbouring street blocks. b. The second group includes four rectangular blocks located behind the eastern blocks of the Salt Market and Water Market. They contained two parallel rows of seven plots each, facing the streets leading out of the markets in an easterly direction, with varying widths. c. Therefore, Morando’s plan encompassed the main elements of the foundation programme mentioned in Jan Zamoyski’s document: the location of the castle and the future church, the division of the city’s space, the layout of the streets with three marketplaces, the division of blocks into plots and the layout of the planned fortifications, curtains and eight bastions123. In the quadrangle intended for the citizens’ buildings, apart from the city hall, which had to be located there, no other public buildings were envisaged124. In the opinion of urban historians, the plan of Zamość, conceived as the basis for the layout of the future city, was distinguished by its outstanding qualities. According to T. Zarębska, “in functional terms it was a correct solution, as for the residents it determined a compact, but not too tight structure of divisions with good shapes and proportions, convenient for buildings of different sizes and standards”125. The plan for the municipal investment on the elevation chosen in the spring of 1579 was ready by the end of the summer of that year. T. Zarębska rightly claims that it was accepted by the chancellor as late as September. Therefore, in a letter of 3 October, he instructed M. Topornicki to send him Morando’s “Painting” and a general project for the development of the immediate area126. In 1579, the future Lwowskie Suburb (Przedmieście Lwowskie, from Lviv) was laid out. This area served as a resource base for the construction of Zamość in the following years. Wooden houses as well as sheds, buildings and temporary structures for the storage of building materials began to be erected on the outlined plots of land, which comprised wooden houses as well as sheds, buildings and temporary structures for the storage of building materials. It was probably still that year that the erection of the Church of the Holy Cross commenced, as well as work on the foundations of the palace on the western side of the promontory intended for the future city. The building materials, mainly wood and bricks, were collected, and research was made as to where they could be obtained. Efforts were also made to engage craftsmen to carry out the construction work, mainly carpenters, earthmovers, masons, blacksmiths and bricklayers. They were recruited by the chancellor himself, by officials in his estates, and later also by his friends who knew his investment plans. The area surrounding Zamość was sparsely wooded. Probably for this reason Zamoyski instructed the administrators of the starosties of Belz, Zamch and Krzeszów, abundant in forests, to prepare timber for building material and deliver it to the site of the investment. Safeguarding himself against the opposition from the subjects of the Zamch starosty that he had experienced earlier, Zamoyski asked the king to issue a mandate ordering them to help with the transport of building timber and firewood for the brickworks and lime kilns. Stephen Báthory issued a relevant document on 11 February 1580129. A month later, on 6 March 1580, Zamoyski’s treasurer Jan Pudłowski, while staying in Warsaw, recorded in the register of revenues and expenditures that a German bricklayer had been sent to the construction site130. The preparatory phase ended with the announcement of the charter on 10 April 1580. During his stay spanning over several weeks, the chancellor also had the opportunity to discuss the details of the investment with B. Morando, M. Topornicki, M. Uhrowiecki, the scribe Jan Piwko and the wojski of Chełm Jakub Snopkowski. The talks also concerned the purchase of villages adjacent to the site of the future city: Janiowice, Szepin, Jarosławiec, Stabrów, Sitaniec and Wola Sitańska, as well as Mokre131.

According to the programme set out in the charter, the city was to be divided into three sectors: government (castle), religious and spiritual (church) and economic (commune of citizens). It was to be organised by Wojciech Wnuk, a Sandomierz citizen and councillor appointed as the locator and vogt on 28 127 AJZ, vol. 1 (as n. 65), no. 349, p. 367, J. Zamoyski do M. Topor- 128 R. The chosen area had to be prepared for new development. Perhaps as early as 1579 or 1580, the plants were removed, the larger undulations filled in and the surface levelled. Only then was the site for the church determined (the area for the palace had been marked out the previous year) and the spatial planning of the city begun. According to A. Miłobędzki, this took place in two approaches: the first one probably in 1581, the second one in July 1583 at the latest. The activities of the first stage were confined to the delimitation of the Great Market and the neighbouring streets, while in the second stage the remaining streets were delimited133. Most of the streets from the east ended at the fourth cross-street, the area beyond was not laid out. Some space was also left to the north, between Szewska Street and the planned fortifications, and similarly to the south beyond the blocks of the southern frontage of the Water Market134. Once the citizens’ quadrangle had been laid out, the process of marking out the town’s fields, meadows and gardens began. This was also carried out in several stages, in the years 1581– 1583, by Franciszek Porowski, a “royal surveyor from the Grodno district” who arrived from Knyszyn. As a result of his work, the Zamość citizens received arable land of 43 lans, 2 morgens and 13 perches, calculated according to the Franconian lan, or approximately 1076 ha135. According to Bronisław Chlebowski, Jan Zamoyski granted a total of 60 lans to Zamość residents136. Further measurement work was carried out in the city area and in the surrounding villages between 1584 and 1586, especially in Żdanów and Kalinovice; perhaps the city area was enlarged137. From 1581, Zamość became a huge construction site. It was then that the most ambitious process of creating an urban centre in Poland began, in many respects the most modern one, especially as far as the composition of the spatial layout and the functional, utilitarian and ideological programme was concerned138. Works on the causeways were intense. In the swampy terrain, they took longer than planned. The construction of the “Żdanów” causeway, which started in 1579, lasted until 1583. In the spring of 1582, the earthmover Maciej Panek began to construct the causeway “towards Płoskie”. These works were prolonged until autumn 1585, and it was only then that the city gained a communication link with the areas to the west, especially with Szczebrzeszyn. The earthmovers then moved on to work on the “side” causeway, to Janiowice, and the “Sitańska” causeway. Commencing the construction of ramparts, coupled with digging moats from the east and north, marked the completion of spatial foundation. The full program of urban spatial division, designated by the founder, was accomplished. Two causeways – to Żdanów and Płoskie – facilitated communication in the southern and western directions. A guard continuously ensured order in the movement of vehicles and pedestrians from the guardhouse erected on the latter causeway in 1585159. The first record of the name of the new center is found in the charter dated 10 April 1580. Jan Zamoyski stated the following: “I give the name Zamoście nad Wieprzcem (Zamość at the Wieprzec river) to this city and castle, in order to distinguish it from our other Zamoście at the Wieprz river”160. Thus, the founder provided the reason for the choice. The aforementioned form – Zamoście – was used four times in 1581: in two letters dated 26 and 30 April, in the nomination of Wojciech Wnuk as the locator and vogt of the newly established city on 28 April, and in the register of army enlistments dated 12 April161. Upon returning from the Pskov expedition, in his letters, he would write “de Zamościo” or “from Zamość” 162, although in a letter to W. Wnuk dated 24 January 1585 he wrote “Zamoście Nowe” (New Zamoście)163. The name was first used by M. Topornicki in his correspondence, for the first time on 22 July 1583164; shortly thereafter, the name was also used by the administration of the estates surrounding the city under construction165. The name “Zamość Nowy” or “Nowy Zamość” was commonly used. In the early 17th c., the second part was omitted, and it was written simply as “Zamość,” occasionally as “Zamoście”. Czopek, Nazwy miejscowe dawnej ziemi chełmskiej i bełskiej (w granicach dzisiejszego państwa polskiego), Wrocław 1988, p. 204; Galicja na According to the decision of King Stephen Báthory outlined in the charter and the founder’s declaration, the basis of the Zamość political system was the municipal law based on Magdeburg’s law, typical of royal cities. Zamoyski decided that only one jurisdiction would apply within the city’s territory, applicable to both citizens and residents of suburbs. He granted them equal rights and privileges, while exempting them from his and his successors’ jurisdiction. The city’s administration was to be entrusted to the municipal council, while justice was to be administered by vogt’s and lay judges’ court. This court, alongside the court of the city council acting as a court of appeal, received the authority to adjudicate and pass judgments on all matters concerning the citizens and other inhabitants. Appeals against the rulings of these courts were supposed to be made to the higher court of German law in Lviv167; the chancellor promised to obtain a guarantee from the authorities in Lviv that they would not burden the appellants from Zamość with “excessive costs”. Drawing inspiration from the organization of the municipal commune in Lviv, in the mid-1580s, he initiated discussions with the authorities of that city, seeking for them to treat Zamość as their colony168. We do not know the details of these negotiations, but it seems that Zamoyski was hardly successful in this matter. The people of Lviv indeed caused difficulties by obstructing the process for the appeals directed to their higher court169. Therefore, the chancellor decided to establish a court of appeal for all his cities and towns under Ordynacja Zamojska (the Zamoyski family entail). He did so in the charter for Zamość issued on 16 October 1601, in the camp near Gowia170. Therefore, the judges were to be delegates from the Ordynacja towns, along with the Zamość burgrave, a law professor from the Academy, and the prelate of the collegiate church. In the extensive charter for this tribunal issued on 24 June 1604 in Zamość, the chancellor slightly altered the composition of the judicial panel. Besides the burgrave, five delegates from the contemporary Ordynacja towns, and the law professor, the Zamość vogt was to replace the prelate. The burgrave was to preside over the court sessions. Judicial terms were scheduled four times a year to commence on 26 January, the day after the Feast of the Ascension, 25 August, and 12 November. The rulings of this court concerning the inhabitants of Ordynacja were to be final and carried the legal force of decrees from the ordynat or lord (Polish title of the entailer, an owner of a majorat), hence its decisions in municipal matters were referred to as edicts171. In this charter, the role of the ordynat as the supreme lord and the source of law was emphasized. The legal status and appeal procedure established in 1604 remained in force until the annexation of Zamość by Austria. In the charter, Zamoyski’s decision, approved by King Stephen, was to appoint the first vogt. He did so on 28 April 1581, naming Wojciech Wnuk to the position for life. Then, Zamoyski appointed four councilors; the lay judges were selected from 1583. The first known election of the city council took place on 16 September 1592. Four elected councilors held the reins of the city’s administration. Each of them served as mayor on a rotating monthly basis. After the death of Wojciech Wnuk in 1605, the vogt was elected annually. The vogt was assisted by a deputy and a bench of seven judges. The first election of councilors and lay judges took place on 9 October 1597 and it was followed by the election of eight guild masters representing the city’s craft guilds. The term of office for city officials was one year. Zamoyski outlined the duties and incomes of the officials in the aforementioned charter issued on 16 October 1601173. Originally, the election was scheduled for the autumn, but considering the complaints from the townspeople about the inconvenience of this timing, Tomasz Zamoyski, by edict dated 29 December 1617, moved it to the last day of the year174. The preserved council books confirm that the elections were indeed held at the end of the year. According to the diary of Bazyli Rudomicz, it is evident that in the years 1657–1572, the elections took place on the last day of the old year or in the first days of the new year175. Only in 1662 was it conducted on 12 January176. In the early decades, councilors also handled the city’s financial affairs. They assumed these responsibilities from 1606 when the period of exemption from rents to the owner expired. From then on, they collected rents and state taxes. Over the following years, in view of many abuses, Tomasz Zamoyski, after assuming full authority in Ordynacja in April 1618, ordered an audit of the city’s accounts and established the office of the tax collector by edict dated 12 July 1621177. This official kept the books of income and expenditure, entering also the rent and tax registers, as well as the records of the committee controlling the accounts on the eve of the election, which was approved by the owner’s delegates to the election178. During the elections, a tax collector and his assistant were also elected (one from the councilors or lay judges, the other from the commoners)179.

The election began with a Holy Mass in the collegiate church, after which the tax collector presented the accounts for the previous year in the city hall. Then, the vogt and four councilors were elected (the owner indicated the first candidate, the common people the second, the vogt with the lay judges the third, and the newly elected councilors the fourth). An instigator, a delegate to the Zamość Tribunal, and a city clerk were also elected180. After the election, all elected officials swore an oath of allegiance and obedience to the owner. After the first partition of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, in the 1780s, the Austrian government embarked on restructuring the political system of Galician cities181. Prior to this, they conducted a verification and approval campaign for the charters and privileges held by the cities. The Governorate in Lviv confirmed Zamość’s privileges in 1783182. The structure of the city’s authorities and the method of their appointment were preserved, with the only change being the relocation of the Zamoyjski Tribunal to Szczebrzeszyn. The Emperor confirmed its operation in 1786, mandating that the assessors have legal education and adjudicate according to Austrian law183. The process of electing authorities, now called management, was similar to that conducted in the past. It was convened at the beginning of the year, usually on 2 January. The offices of vogt, four councilors, seven lay judges, a delegate to the Tribunal, and the so-called “senior civitatis” who supervised the proper functioning of the administration and confirmed the elections, were maintained. Then the name of the treasurer and the deputy vogt were announced. After the elections, the new officials swore allegiance to the owner, administered by two of his representatives, secular and ecclesiastical184.

Shortly after the election (usually within a week), another assembly, called “convocatio publica”, was convened, during which six assessors were elected to assess the property of the townspeople and suburban residents. Seven deputies were chosen to collect dues (rents and taxes). Six inspectors of measures, weights, and chimney condition were appointed. Additionally, as needed, an instigator was selected to oversee order in the city185. From 1785 onwards, the city’s security was managed by a police corporal and six policemen, who were subordinate to the precinct court. They also supervised the prison and ensured that innkeepers had obtained permission for “playing music”186. In the 1770s, the treasurer, at the expense of the townspeople, appointed four guards from among Christians and Jews to serve during the night hours. They were tasked with guarding the city against fires and stopping anyone appearing on the 180 APL (as n. 10), Acta Consularia Zamoscensia (hereinafter as: 181 S. A two-stage election of officials was introduced, establishing so-called Departments. These were to be formed through election, with one member of the Department representing twenty voters, who were property owners in the city. These Department members were to oversee city accounts, approve budgets, and elect officials for a four-year term: the mayor, who also served as a judge, two councilors, known as assessors, a syndic, a treasurer, a clerk, a police corporal, six policemen, and a city bailiff. The precinct authorities appointed the police director, who also served as a quartermaster188. From 1794, these offices were held for life189. Another change in the structure of the administration occurred in 1804. In addition to the mayor, syndic, treasurer, clerk, and two secretaries, three counselors (replacing assessors) and three police inspectors were appointed. Therefore, law enforcement services were increased190. After 1785, courts were divided into civil and criminal. A separate criminal court, dealing with cases punishable by imprisonment, was also established in Zamość in 1787191. It is worth mentioning that after the confirmation of Zamość’s privileges in 1783, the occupying authorities ordered the use of the image of Saint Thomas the Apostle with a spear as the emblem and coat of arms, as stipulated in the founding charter, and the removal of other previously depicted elements, especially the “Jelita” coat of arms192.

After the incorporation of Galician territories into the Duchy of Warsaw, initially, the Austrian-era authorities continued to officiate. By the decree of the Duke of Warsaw, Frederick Augustus I, dated 24 February 1810, these lands were brought under the constitution of the Duchy dated 22 July 1807, which broke with the principles of estate law and introduced universal law193. The decree of Frederick Augustus I, dated 23 February 1809, abolished the political system of towns based on German law, including the Magdeburg variant in Zamość. In Zamość this decision was only implemented in June 1811194. The administration was held by the mayor, appointed by the Duke of Warsaw, and he was subordinate to the sub-prefect in the district. He was assisted by honorary lay judges, also appointed by the central authorities. The local government body was the city council, consisting of nine members, who convened with the mayor. He was obliged to execute its resolutions regarding the entirety of urban life195. The judicial system, both organizationally and in terms of jurisdiction, based on the French model, was a component of the general court system. A peace court was established, located in Szczebrzeszyn. It consisted of two chambers: conciliatory and contentious. The latter adjudicated criminal cases punishable by up to five days of arrest or a fine of 30 złotys. Criminal cases punishable by imprisonment for up to five years were judged by correctional police courts; one of two such courts in the department operated in Zamość. From 15 August 1810, criminal cases carrying a penalty of more than five years of imprisonment were adjudicated by the criminal court in Lublin197. After the occupation of Zamość by the Russian army in November 1813, its existing authorities continued their activities. However, their structure and competencies were changed only by the constitution of the Kingdom of Poland, granted by Tsar Alexander I198. In the charter, Jan Zamoyski declared that he had decided to build a residence combined with a city, surrounded by fortifications and a moat “with regard to the safety and benefit not only of myself and my friends, but of the entire neighbourhood and the subjects from neighboring villages”. Confirming this act in Vilnius on 12 June 1580, King Stephen Báthory stated that the founder did it “also for the benefit of the Commonwealth and the people neighboring this place”199. In the royal charter, the king added that he supported this initiative as beneficial for the common good. It was in the interest of the Commonwealth to have as many populous and defensible “well-built” cities as possible, especially located near the borders, where they can serve as a refuge for the nobility and other subjects. Batory also declared the monarchy’s steadfast commitment to supporting similar undertakings200. The chosen location for the future Zamość was within the range of Tatar raids, against which the fortress was to secure the people living in the vicinity, as well as those from further away. In 1583, earthworks on the Żdanowska causeway were completed, and in 1585, on the second one, towards the west, as well. The terrain was leveled for construction purposes, and necessary drainage works were carried out around the hill. Ponds and wells were dug to replace those flooded by the Great Flood202. The commencement of works on the embankments in 1584 suggests that perhaps in the following year, due to the impossibility of expanding the area designated for construction, a decision was made to change the original concept of the city. This included abandoning one bastion in the north and constructing a deformed bastion in its place. Some adjustments were also introduced to the spatial layout203. In the following years, ditches were dug and embankments were piled up. In addition to earthmovers, peasants from various estates were also employed to transport materials and spread earth on the embankments204. In 1587, the Lubelska Gate, leading to Lublin and also to Janiowice (thus its name), was built, for which the blacksmith Prokop made hinges205. After Archduke Maximilian entered through it to the city in 1588, it was bricked up. In the following years, two other gates were erected, which were of a provisional nature. The embankments were completed by 1592, but work on them continued until the end of the century206. At the same time, construction began on fortifications measuring over 2.500 meters in circumference, comprising seven bastions connected by curtains ranging in length from 160 to 230 meters. The embankment was encased externally with a limestone wall measuring 11–12 meters in height, 2.4 meters thick at the base, and 1.6 meters thick at the top. On the side facing the moat, a stone wall with a slanted parapet were laid, protecting a 2-meter-wide firing shelf on which the defenders were to stand. Below ran a rampart road. The scarps, about 1 meter wide and 4–4.5 meters long, connected by vaults, reinforced the wall from the inside. At the base, the thickness of the rampart and the wall was about 7 meters. The moats were several meters wide and about 6 meters deep207.

Along with the curtains, bastions were constructed – four regular ones, while the shape of the remaining ones depended on the terrain conditions. Bastion II (southern), which was open and flattened, bordered the edge of Wielka Zalewa. Bastion III was built as two small, irregular structures because the unstable ground did not allow for the construction of a regular bastion. Only at the end of the 17th c., one bastion was erected in their place, significantly extending into the neighbouring marshy areas. In the quadrangle of the city, on the Horodelska Street, which around 1603 was renamed to Żydowska, a Jewish synagogue was erected, along with a school, a Jewish hospital, and a bathhouse. The city hall began to be built before 1591 in the western frontage of the northern side of the Great Market. This untypical location was to ensure that the city hall will not obstruct the view from the castle to the Market and would not limit both main compositional axes of Zamość225. A tower was built alongside it, protruding in front of the facade. In the late 16th c., mason Michał Belther, under Morando’s command, reinforced its walls226. The preserved statistics from the Austrian authorities do not list the types of buildings. They indicate a total of 841 structures in the city and its suburbs as of 1808238. Outside the citizens’ quadrangle, churches, and the so-called “weapons square”, partially built-up in the first half of the 17th c., mention should be made of the markets. The Great Market, along with the multi-storey buildings on its frontage and the city hall, with intersecting compositional axes in its centre, acquired the character of an “urban spatial salon”241. The Salt Market was the main hub of trade, weekly markets, and fairs. On the side facing the town hall, numerous craft stalls and booths were located; until 1636, they also stood around the walls of the exchange building242. The role of the Water Market is less known. T. Zarębska argued that it was supposed to serve as a residential place and never had a commercial character 243, but it was probably used for trade during fairs. The three places near the city gates were not directly associated with the main compositional theme of the city. Each of them was linked to one important landmark: the place near the Lwowska Gate was associated with the exchange, later with the Franciscan church; the one near the Lubelska Gate (Janowicka) was linked to the Academy, while the one near the Szczebrzeska Gate was associated with the collegiate church. Nevertheless, the main communication route led from the west to east from Szczebrzeska Gate through the Grodzka Street, the Great Market and the Lwowska Street to the Lwowska Gate244.

The suburbs surrounded intra-mural Zamość on the east, north and west. They were established on about 42 Franconian lans, which is around 1050 hectares. The first to be planned was the Lwowskie Suburb in 1579, which served as a preparatory base for the construction of Zamość in the following years245. It seems to have been incorporated into the city area even before 1648, as it is recorded in the extent of 1653251. In 1696, there were 12 mud huts recorded there. Their inhabitants were treated as peasants and were expected to clean the streets of mud and filth as part of their serfdom status. They were also assigned other tasks252. The normal rhythm of economic activity of the suburbs was abruptly ended by the Northern War of 1702–1718, which brought further destructions253.

The predominantly wooden houses in the city, as well as the entirely wooden construction in the suburbs, along with the use of wood in the construction of stone buildings and other structures, posed a fire hazard. Before 1648, four fires broke out in Zamość. The first, about which little is known, occurred on 22 June 1623257. Four years later, on 6 June 1627 in the afternoon, a fire broke out in the Salt Market, engulfing adjacent citizens’ houses and buildings of the Academy. The dormitory, printing house, and buildings near the castle were destroyed. The fire spread to the Lubelskie Suburb and consumed many houses. In total, about 100 houses were burned down258. In the next major fire, in 1633, the Academy and many buildings in the eastern part of the city burned down259. Contrary to claims made in numerous works about Zamość, the fire did not engulf the collegiate church260. The fire of 1639 was mentioned in a request made by Katarzyna Zamoyska, widow of Tomasz, submitted on behalf of the citizens at the Chełm sejmik on 9 July 1641. She asked for partial exemption from state taxes261. Fires were particularly frequent in the third quarter of the 17th c. After the burning of the suburbs before the arrival of Cossack and Tatar troops on 5 November 1648, the economic life there was disrupted for a longer period. Many refugees, mainly nobles, gathered in the fortress. After more than sixty years of development and consolidation of urban functions, surrounded by modern bastion fortifications, Zamość entered a period of unrest and wars. Following the outbreak of the uprising in Ukraine in June 1648, defensive preparations began: citizens and a garrison of about 100 soldiers were trained, and food and ammunition gathered. Refugees from the southeastern lands, nobles, and monks began to flock to the fortress. After the defeats of the Polish troops and the siege of Lviv by Chmielnicki, it was expected that he would march further towards Zamość. In September, the castellan of Elbląg, Ludwik Wejher, arrived with 300 cavalry and 1200 infantry. He assumed command of the fortress and started preparations for its defense282. Knowing about the march of the Cossack-Tatar armies, on 5 November all suburbs were burned down. The citizens allowed the fire to consume 459 houses and cottages. Both gates were barricaded and cannons were placed on them, leaving only a small entrance at the Szczebrzeska Gate for communication283. On 6 November, Chmielnicki arrived in łabuńki, where he established his headquarters, and his forces surrounded Zamość. The besiegers dug through the Szczebrzeska causeway and released water from the Great Reservoir. They commenced artillery bombardment, preparing for the assault, and on the night of 9 November they unsuccessfully attacked from the Lubelskie Suburb. Subsequently, Chmielnicki decided to blockade the fortress, refraining from a general assault; eventually, he approached the defenders with a ransom proposal. The negotiated amount was set at 20 thousand złoty, and on 21 November, after reaching an agreement, the besiegers began to retreat towards Krasnystaw and Chełm284. The intramural city did not suffer significant damage. However, it was overcrowded with refugees, facing shortages of food, as well as fodder for about 1500 horses. The horses, along with the cattle brought in, began to perish. Diseases spread among the defenders. The initial military attempt to defend the fortress did not go exceptionally well285. The burning of the suburbs led to the disruption of economic life for a longer period, although once the threat passed, the residents embarked on the reconstruction of their houses and infrastructure used for economic activity.
