The Swedes, with a force of 18,000 troops and 40 cannons, approached Zamość on 25 February. They summoned Jan II Zamoyski to defect to their side and surrender the fortress286. Firmly supporting Jan Kazimierz, Zamoyski refused, and on 27 February the the Swedes began bombarding the city with cannons, which lasted all night. They killed one ox and wounded a man, as Rudomicz wrote287. For two more days, they urged Zamoyski through envoys to surrender, but he continued to refuse. They departed on 1 March, burning buildings in the suburbs and surrounding villages288. The city hall tower, the Franciscan church and 10 tenements were damaged289. Zamość gained renown as one of the three places in Poland – alongside Gdańsk and Jasna Góra – unoccupied by the Swedes. Anxieties increased in the autumn of 1656 due to the return of the Tatars to the Crimea, who were ravaging the vicinity. An epidemic began to spread, but it did not affect Zamość. The city anxiously followed news of Swedish activities, as they were joined by Prince George II Rákóczi of Transylvania and the Cossacks, who entered the Commonwealth in January 1657. After an attempt to capture Lviv, Rákóczi headed towards Cracow. Zamość remained under threat as Rákóczi moved from there to meet the Swedish king in Zawichost. The combined Swedish-Hungarian forces planned to seize Zamość and Brest-Litovsk in April. In Zamość, preparations for defense were underway, with strengthened guards and the accumulation of food and fodder for horses290. On 19 April, it was decided to demolish houses in the suburbs291. In May, the threat passed as the allies headed north. It wasn’t until July that the danger increased again when rumours spread about Rakoczy’s return to Hungary. His army appeared south of the fortress on 8 July, beyond the pond – as Rudomicz wrote, they were responsible for many arson attacks in the vicinity of the city292, For the residents of Zamość and the refugees gathered in the fortress, it was the end of the war293.

The next period of destruction was brought about by the Northern War. Before the arrival of General Magnus Stenbock’s troops on 11 February 1703, the suburbs were burned on the orders of Anna z Gnińskich, the widow of Marcin Zamoyski294. The Swedes remained in the vicinity of Zamość for a week, burning down the liberty of the Franciscan monastery, named Podtopole, which was already located outside the city limits, and plundering neighboring settlements295. In late September of the following year, the main Swedish forces under the leadership of Charles XII approached Zamość. Two weeks after their departure, on 21 October, Cossack units appeared near Zamość but were repelled by the reassembled garrison, although they caused damage in the surrounding area. On 17 December, Saxon units arrived, committing numerous robberies and ravages. They approached Zamość again in February 1705, imposing a contribution and demanding food supplies. On 17 November 1705, Cossack units under the command of Hetman Ivan Mazepa once again reached the fortress, intending to occupy it on behalf of Tsar Peter I and King Augustus II the Strong. By agreement with the ordynat, 1000 Russian infantrymen led by Polish Colonel Zbigniew Przypkowski were allowed in the following day, later replaced by Saxon General Joachim Bernard Kyan in January 1706. During his stay, he demanded “provisions for the kitchen”, costing the residents of Zamość 28 thalers per month. He demanded 100 thalers monthly and the city council met them. The Russians left Zamość at the end of May, while the Saxon general departed in mid-June 1706297.

In the autumn of 1706, perhaps at the behest of the Tsar, who did not trust Augustus II, the Russian general Baur attempted to seize the fortress by trickery. He exploited an invitation to the palace issued on 8 December by Teresa z Potockich, wife of ordynat. He arrived the next day, hoping to take advantage at departure to capture the Lwowska Gate and occupy the city. He likely gained the favor of the commanding officer Major Tauben and had previously ordered his units to approach the gate. Upon opening the gate, Baur’s grenadiers rushed towards the departing carriage, cut off its team, and then breached the walls, reaching the ramparts and turning the cannons towards the city. What the Russians failed to accomplish in 1706, the Saxons achieved in 1715 when they captured Zamość. Saxon troops led by Field Marshal Flemming marched from Warsaw marched against the forces of the Tarnogród Confederation formed on 26 November 1715. After crossing the Vistula in Sandomierz on 8 December, they attacked the confederates, who withdrew to Zamość and deployed in the suburbs and surrounding villages. Although the parties agreed to a week-long ceasefire on 24 December, the Saxons broke it the next day. A battle was averted as mediators sent by Chancellor Szembek halted the Saxon advance and persuaded the confederates to withdraw from the vicinity of Zamość. Two days later Saxon troops reached the walls of the fortress, demanding entry, but the ordynat refused. Flemming insisted that his officers be allowed to make necessary purchases inside. For this purpose, the gate at the Szczebrzeska Gate, then called Lubelska Gate, was to be opened daily, with continuous movement observed there under the supervision of the Saxon guard. On the morning of 28 December, when Saxon troops stood by the gate, a group of officers staying in Zamość overpowered the gate guards, unlocked it, and opened it. The waiting soldiers entered the city. After a brief fight in which Captain Roman was mortally wounded, the Saxons seized Zamość. Treating the fortress as their spoil, they looted the citizens and and the gathered nobility, taking all the stored deposits. They also confiscated the movables found in Zamość belonging to the Confederates, and tax collectors from the Chełm Land took 3,000 złoty from the deposits held by the citizens. Flemming released some prisoners for ransom, but about 40 were kept under lock and key. Leaving Colonel La Serre with a garrison in the fortress, the field marshal and his army left Zamość on 31 December. During their six-month stay, the Saxon garrison carried out numerous looting and requisitions, demanding provisions and money for lavish living. When leaving in July 1716, the Saxons took all the ammunition from the fortress’s arsenal and many cannons298. Zamość took a long time to return to normal life. The damages inflicted on the city and its outskirts by Polish, Russian, Saxon, and Cossack forces were estimated at 106,752 Polish zloty in 1718299.

Zamość suffered further destruction and losses only in the years 1809 and 1813. Until then, the unreinforced fortress walls were deteriorating. There were also changes in the hydrographic system, especially on the western side, where the Zalewa Mała turned into marshy meadows. It was only during the 1809 war that the Austrians became interested in Zamość, planning to establish one of their military supply depots there. In March 1809, Colonel Engineer Ferdynand von Pulszky was sent there to prepare the fortress for defense. For a month he supervised wall repairs and cleaning of the moats. A rampart was built in front of the Szczebrzeska Gate, and the causeway was damaged [uszkodzono groblę – na pewno tak miało być?]. The military quarters and ammunition and provision warehouses were prepared for the purpose of arriving troops300. In early May, Prince Józef Poniatowski with the main part of the Polish forces began a march into Austrian territory. The vanguard of one of columns of these armies reached the vicinity of the fortress on 15 May. Its commander, General Ignacy Kamieński, called on the Austrians to surrender the next day. The Austrians refused. Shortly thereafter, the defenders set fire to the suburbs along the Szczebrzeska road, followed by the Lubelskie Suburb and partially the Lwowskie Suburb301. On the evening of 17 May, General Jan Pelletier arrived at the fortress with a battalion of the 2nd Infantry Regiment, a sapper company, and six cannons. The next day, they positioned them closer than 600 meters from the Szczebrzeska Gate and began shelling. One of the grenades set fire to the ordynat’s stables. Meanwhile, fires started breaking out in the city; a food warehouse burned down. The fires were set by residents, engaging in sabotage in favour of the besiegers302. On the evening of next day, reinforcements arrived at the walls, and preparations for the assault began. A plan of attack envisaged involvement of about 2000 soldiers. They were to advance in five columns. The main thrust was directed towards the section of fortifications between the III and IV bastions, as well as towards the Lubelska Gate303. Auxiliary diversionary actions were to be conducted in front of the two remaining gates. The assault was scheduled for 12:30 a.m. on 20 May, but due to delays in occupying the starting positions by some units, it was postponed to 2:15 a.m. From 10:30 p.m., diversionary tactics were initiated at the Lwowska Gate, where artillery fire was directed and houses on the outskirts, spared from the previous fire, were also set ablaze304. The assault lasted just under two hours, and by around 4 a.m., Zamość was captured by the Poles. During the siege, five buildings near the palace burned down, over 100 others were partially destroyed (with burnt roofs, damaged doors and door frames, shattered roof tiles, and collapsed ceilings). In the suburbs, 440 houses were burned. The most affected were the Szczebrzeskie and Lwowskie Suburbs, where only six houses survived, while relatively fewer damages were inflicted on the Lubelskie Suburb, especially on łanowa Street. Additionally, two brickworks within the castle walls and a slaughterhouse behind the Lubelska Gate were also burned down. The day after the assault, the right front of Bastion IV collapsed, which was built on filled marshes305.

A few days after the capture of Zamość, Colonel Jean Baptiste Mallet de Grandville, a Frenchman and the head of engineering troops of the Duchy of Warsaw, arrived at the fortress. After inspecting it on 25 May, he supervised the reparation of the damages to the walls and suggested bringing the fortress to a defensible state. The works lasted for over three years and were only completed during the siege in 1813. They were overseen by Captain, later Lieutenant Colonel of artillery, Leonard Jodko-Narkiewicz306. The preparations for the expedition to Russia in 1812 were not interrupted. After the defeat of Napoleon’s army, it became clear that the advancing Russian forces would reach Zamość following the retreating French army. On 22 January 1813, the headquarters of the Duchy of Warsaw’s ordered the army to besiege the fortress. The defenders started to gather food and fodder and build entrenchments and redoubts in the outer defenses. In early February, the commander General Maurycy Hauke ordered that wooden houses in the city, especially between bastions V and VI, were dismantled, and from the materials obtained, barracks and guardhouses were built on the fortifications outside the walls. Only on 25 February was a battery erected near the mill, and the causeway to Płoski and the water sluice near it were reinforced with palisades307. 298 Ibidem, p. 83–86. 299 R. A regular siege commenced. It did not resemble the siege of 1809. The besiegers did not dare to launch an assault on the fortress. Instead, the fighting took place on the outskirts, while the fortress endured nine months of artillery bombardment. In April the bombardment lasted for thirteen days308. The defenders removed wooden roofs from the arsenal and other buildings, as well as from houses and tenements, covering some of them with earth. They dismantled wooden houses to have wood for making fires at night at the outposts. By the end of September, when there was a shortage of houses to dismantle, the commander ordered all the linden trees to be cut down309. In November, the food supplies ran out, and the cattle and horses started to be eaten. The Fortress Defense Council agreed to negotiate surrender. The talks began on 20 November and four days later a convention was signed, backdated to 22 November. Out of the garrison initially consisting of 3,812 people, 1,378 soldiers and officers left on November 25 under their own power, while 891 remained in the hospitals310.

The city and its suburbs suffered serious damage. Over 70 wooden houses were demolished or burned during the bombardment, while masonry buildings were damaged by artillery fire. Affected structures included the city hall, collegiate church, palace and adjacent buildings. The suburbs lost around 160 houses along with their outbuildings, some of which were completely destroyed by fire. Additionally, three brickworks, the city slaughterhouse, and the house of the dog catcher in Podgroble Żdanowskie (a settlement in southern part of the Lwowskie Suburb, next to the causeway leading to Żdanów village) were burned down. Wólka Miejska (formerly known as Wólka Kalinowicka, a settlement of a dozen or so farms, bordering the Lwowskie Suburb to the east) and Podtopole were also destroyed by fire. Nearby villages such as Kalinowice, Żdanów, and Janowice were also ruined. The population decreased by 40%311. During the times of the Duchy of Warsaw, the city gradually shifted its functions. After the transfer of the centre of Ordynacja to Zwierzyniec in 1806, the economic role of Zamość weakened, and the citizens became poorer. Instead, it was the military function that began to be dominant, which continued to develop in the following years. The number of inhabitants is always a crucial factor in characterizing the functions of a city. Making use of the number of houses provided above, we can estimate the population growth of Zamość by using the commonly accepted demographic ratio: 6 people per 1 house, and adding 10% for untaxed individuals to the obtained number312. After the wars ended, the city slowly returned to normal life. However, the emerging prospects were not favorable. Impoverished citizens continued to struggle with debts, as did the municipal authorities. The social discipline was weak. Frequent disputes arose over municipal obligations and the amount of taxes. Jews demonstrated great economic activity, gradually dominating trade and also engaging in craftsmanship. Their numbers increased from 300 in 1692 to 1,000 people in 1770. The impoverishment of the burghers contributed to the ruin of the city’s buildings. The urban community of Zamość began to form from the moment the first settlers arrived. In the charter, the founder decided that only Roman Catholics could settle in the city. Therefore, those who settled in Zamość between 1581 and 1585 were former residents of Chodel, Chęciny, Garwolin, Gdańsk, Kazimierz Dolny, Lublin, Lviv, Mogielnica, Opatów, Sandomierz, Sulejów, Toruń, Warszawa and Wojsławice326. The merchants, able to engage in extensive international trade, made for only a small group within them. Hence, on 30 April 1585, the chancellor allowed Armenians to settle, “so that the city founded by me might more easily prosper and enrich itself through trade”327. The Armenians were allocated plots along the eastern and northern sides of the Great Market and along the street continuing from it. East of this street, a square was designated where they were to construct their temple and associated buildings. The chancellor also promised to assign them fields, gardens, and meadows in the suburbs, just like other citizens had them assigned328. The Jews also sought the right to settle in Zamość. Sephardic Jews received the privilege to settle on 26 February 1588. Zamoyski granted them plots on Szewska Street and at the Salt Market, guaranteeing religious freedom and support in their affairs329. The third organized ethnic group settled in Zamość were the Greeks. J. Zamoyski had contacts with their representatives, both traders from the Turkish territories and residents of Lviv. In 1586, he asked the city council of Lviv to resolve the matter of a resident of Lviv, Michał the Greek, and Seropel from Candia, Crete347. Two years later, he supported the case of Pro- kop Syropopulo, whom he presented as a merchant and citizen of Zamość348, It is possible that he was the same Seropel who settled in Zamość. he chancellor announced permission for Greeks to settle in his new city in a privilege dated 10 January 1589349; From this document we can infer that members of this group did not intend to create a separate community. The extent of 1591 lists 12 properties owned by Greeks. In the following years, their number undoubtedly increased. Taking advantage of the permission granted in the privilege, they built their wooden church. After 1606, it became the seat of the Ruthenian brotherhood of the Protection of the Mother of God. In 1618, at the initiative of T. Zamoyski, construction of a stone church began, which survived until 1631350. The community was subject to the Patriarch of Constantinople. The history of the Greek colony in Zamość is not well known. Its members traded mainly in wine, constantly encountering difficulties in relations with Lviv. In the second half of the 17th c., especially during conflicts with Turkey, the Greeks left Zamość. Their temple was taken over by the Disunites (the Orthodox in Poland who did not adhere to decisions of the Union of Brest in 1596, anti-Uniates) and later by the Basilian monks.

Migrants from the British Isles, especially Scots, stood out from among other ethnic groups. They formed an Anglo-Scottish trading colony in the first half of the 17th c. By the mid-century, there were 25 Scots living in Zamość, with another twenty residing there temporarily351. They also engaged primarily in trade. They lived on both the western and eastern sides of the Great Market and at adjacent streets352. It is worth mentioning that in the late 16th c., a Scottish clergyman, soldier, diplomat, and humanist named William Bruce worked as a professor of Roman law at the Academy353. Therefore, a multiethnic, multicultural, and multireligious urban community was forming in Zamość, attracting attention due to its distinctive attire, customs, and language. Foreigners engaged in long-distance trade, and some, mainly Scots, were local market traders. Others, especially Germans brought from cities in Pomerania and Prussia, were involved in crafts. While craftsmanship was crucial during the city’s construction, it somewhat diminished in importance later. It is crucial to emphasize that in the functional concept of Zamość, compared to trade, craftsmanship was assigned a secondary role. It was not allocated a specific sector in the spatial layout, but rather plots outside the center, along streets near the fortifications, and this tendency persisted throughout the examined period354. The growing number of Jewish residents in Zamość, involved in crafts, along with the decline in the significance of guild organizations, led to an increase in the number of non-guild craftsmen, especially in the food and clothing sectors, both among Jews and Christians370. Until 1772, Zamość had guilds for beef butchers (established in 1588), cobblers (1585), furriers, and metal crafts (established in 1590), clothiers (1605), potters (1610), leather crafts, such as saddlers (1614), tailors (1614), blacksmiths (1618), bakers (1619), weavers (1620), brewers (1644), pork butchers (1690), and tanners (1698). During the Austrian partition period, in 1778, carpenters and bricklayers formed an association, and in 1786, two butcher guilds merged into one organization371. There was also a guild of barber-surgeons, organized in 1622372. After the city was occupied by Austria, the new authorities aimed to organize the craft guilds, eliminate conflicts among their members, and adapt existing organizational forms to the needs of the Austrian economic system. In 1776, Jews were allowed to engage in crafts for the needs of their own community, and from 1789 onwards, they could practice any trade on equal terms with Christians373. After several years of preparations, the “General Regulations of Guilds” were developed and announced in 1777, including a standardized statute. Existing associations were required to adjust their organization and activities to the provisions contained therein. Only after fulfilling this requirement did Emperor Francis II approve the functioning of 13 guilds in Zamość in 1796374.

At the same time, the authorities sought to attract craftsmen from German countries as part of a colonization campaign. The first stage, in 1774, resulted in only a few masters arriving. It was only during the second stage, under Joseph II, that 28 colonists from Prussia specializing in food, clothing, and leather trades settled, purchasing houses at auctions or building them in the suburbs375. However, this action did not yield the expected results due to limited demand for artisanal products. The number of craftsmen barely increased in the early 19th c., as in 1804, there were 289 of them living in the city and its suburbs, and in 1808, there were 274 craftsmen376. Since the founding of the city, craft workshops were located in the suburbs. The first brickyard was likely built in the Lwowskie Suburb after the arrival of a cooper from Warsaw in 368 K. During the Austrian partition times, the production of spirits was taken over by the Zamoyski family entail. At that time, there were two mills: one by the Zamość pond with four grindstones, and the other in Janowice with two grindstones, where mainly Jews ground grain into flour and malt. Additionally, there were two breweries: one large brewery in Zamość and another in Żdanów, as well as several distilleries. Earlier, one of the ordynats built a slaughterhouse in the Lubelskie Suburb394. Trade was the most important economic activity. The founder of Zamość understood this and emphasized his intention to organize the city as a trade centre that would be significant not only locally but in the entire Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and beyond. The founder’s efforts can be divided into three categories. The first consisted of granting privileges favorable to Zamość, ensuring the rapid development of trade. From King Stephen Báthory Zamoyski obtained the confirmation of the calendar of fairs, which took place in winter, late spring, and autumn395. After twenty years, when it became apparent that this was not sufficient, in 1600, he received from King Sigismund III a privilege to organize a fair on Saint Victorian’s Day (5 September), which was intended as a continuation of the great summer fair in Jarosław, held in the second half of August, but also as its competition396. The weekly market was set for Wednesday, and when it turned out that one day was not enough, in 1588, he asked King Sigismund III to confirm the charter from 1585 and grant a second weekly market on Saturday397. The fairs were to last for 16 days and were to follow the model of annual gatherings in Lublin and Toruń. Their schedule was linked to the annual meetings of merchants in Chełm, Lublin, Jarosław, and Lviv. Zamość received incomplete staple rights binding merchants going from the Chełm Land, Volhynia, the Belz Voivodeship, and Lviv to the west and north of the country with agricultural and forest products, saltpeter, hops, and salt, as well as with merchants travelling from all these directions and Gdańsk with all sorts of merchandise. The merchants were obligated to unload and offer goods for sale in the city for three days. As a result, Zamość, which had previously been on the sidelines of the main trade routes, became an important hub. This also applied to communication routes between Lublin and Lviv,

Earlier, two routes were frequented between these cities: one led through Bychawa, Turobin, Szczebrzeszyn, Lubaczów, and the other through Krasnystaw, Grabowiec, Hrubieszów, or Tyszowce to Belz. In the following decades after the establishment of Zamość, an intermediate route began to operate, much shorter, leading from Szczebrzeszyn or Krasnystaw to Zamość and further through Tyszowce to Belz or Potylicz398. The course of this route was changing in the early 17th c., after the establishment of Żółkiew, Rawa Ruska, and Tomaszów399. In the charter, King Stephen Báthory permanently exempted the citizens of Zamość from paying customs duties within the Commonwealth on land and water. He also provided significant discounts on paying main and border customs duties for ten years and established a customs chamber in Zamość400. These freedoms undoubtedly interested both domestic and foreign merchants, encouraging them to settle in Zamość. Among foreigners, these were mainly Greeks, Armenians, and Jews engaged in trade with cities in the Ottoman Empire. This direction was associated with the second category of efforts by the founder, who aimed to make his city an important centre of trade with the East. However, a major obstacle was posed by the powerful city of Lviv, which guarded its trading monopolies. The chancellor attempted to negotiate with the Lviv city council to recognize Zamość as their colony, but it seems he achieved little success401. Nonetheless, in the following decades, under the protection of its owners, Zamość emerged as a significant hub of trade exchange along routes leading eastward and southward402. The privileges and freedoms also encouraged merchants from Western and Southern Europe to settle in Zamość, as mentioned in the characterization of the urban community. The founder, as well as officials from the Podolian estates and numerous leased royal domains, promoted the Zamość fairs among merchants engaged in long-distance trade. Zamoyski also wrote letters to cities participating in this trade regarding this matter403. At the turn of the 16th and 17th c., the chancellor also undertook efforts to make his city an important centre of cattle trade404. In 1600, he obtained a privilege to organize a fair on St. Victorian’s Day, entered into agreements with merchants for the delivery of cattle to Zamość, and guaranteed their repurchase if they were not sold there405. Thanks to these efforts, Zamość welcomed numerous groups of merchants, while its citizens, benefiting from the support of their owners, developed extensive trade contacts in Poland and travelled abroad to Moscow, the Czech lands, Hungary and Turkey.

The third category of Zamoyski’s efforts was related to quickly connecting the elevated terrain chosen for the city’s foundation with the roads in the vicinity. Between 1579 and 1585, three causeways were built to provide access to it. The chancellor and his officials particularly focused on the causeway leading to Płoskie, which allowed access to Szczebrzeszyn and further west and north of the country, while also connecting Zamość with one of the Lublin-Lviv routes. The chancellor’s actions aimed at making his city a centre of domestic and international trade were successful. Zamość, benefiting from the patronage of the founder and his son Tomasz, emerged as such a centre, known among merchants within the Commonwealth and beyond406. The trade of Zamość developed in three zones. The first was the local market, covering the territory within a distance of up to 20 km, where most villages belonged to the Zamoyski family entail. It made contact between the peasants living in these villages and the estate’s centre easier. The second zone was the regional market, primarily consisting of towns within the entail, which had extensive contacts with Zamość merchants. Merchants from older towns in the vicinity, both royal and private, also established connections, such as those from Krasnystaw, Kraśnik, Skierbieszów, Grabowiec, Hrubieszów, Tyszowce, Lubaczów, Krasnobród, Biłgoraj, and later also merchants from newer towns like Cieszanów, Florianów, Rawa Ruska, Tomaszów, Płazów, and Lipsk. In the first half of the 17th c., the trade exchange of this region was concentrated in Zamość, which replaced older towns in its vicinity as the main centre in the long-distance trade, reaching markets in Poznań, Gniezno, Toruń, Gdańsk, Warsaw, Brest, Lublin, Chełm, and Lviv. We can therefore speak of the formation of three regional markets on the border in the second quarter of the 17th c.: Cracow, Lublin, and Lviv, as well as the regional market of Zamość407. During this period, Zamość merchants maintained extensive trade contacts with foreign cities, from Lisbon to Moscow, from Stockholm to Istanbul and Bursa, and even with cities in Persia408.

The wars of the mid-17th and early 18th c. hindered the prosperous development of Zamość’s trade. During times of unrest, some foreign merchants began to leave the city. Cities such as Poznań, Gniezno, Cracow, Sandomierz, and Lublin also lost their significance in international trade. A new route from the west began to function, especially from Silesia – after crossing the Vistula River, it led through Urzędów or Kraśnik to Szczebrzeszyn and Zamość, further to Volhynia or Lviv. Zamość’s role was determined by the fame of itsfortress; as a result, the city’s connections with Silesia remained continuous and intensive for a long time409. However, the exchange in the regional and local markets weakened due to the impoverishment of society, including the citizens of Zamość. In the 18th c., Zamość’s role in international trade was only a memory. This was due to changes in the organization of international trade and the decline in the importance of fairs. Zamość became a city of small merchants and craftsmen catering to the needs of the local market and a narrow circle of customers from the Ordynacja’s court, who also imported necessary goods without the mediation of Zamość merchants410. The trade exchange with the towns and villages of Ordynacja was taken over by Jews, who received the right to conduct trade on Sundays from the ordynat Michał Zdzisław in 1732. In 1738, due to a decline in the number of Armenians, the activity of their community was suspended411. After the first partition of Poland, the trade crisis deepened. Although the Austrians attempted to link Galicia with other provinces of the state, the efforts were hindered by high customs duties. Agricultural products, animals, and craft goods, imported from Bohemia, Bavaria, and Prussia, were sold at two markets per week and four fairs per year. In addition to the Salt Market and adjacent slaughterhouses, goods were displayed on stalls in the arcades and in the suburbs of the town412. Since the late 16th c., guesthouses continuously hosted guests. They served alcoholic beverages. Unfortunately, determining their exact number is challenging. We only know that in 1692, there were 18 such establishments in the city413. Information about their activities comes from oaths taken by the city council after fires. In the years 1664–1665, 22 such guesthouses on Kozacka and Kowalska Streets and 16 on Lwowska Street were destroyed by fire414. In 1672, during three fires, 7 guesthouses in the city burned down, while in the Lwowskie Suburb and on Kozacka Street, 25 were destroyed, and in Nowy Świat as many as 37 were affected415. In 1677, a fire destroyed 15 such guesthouses in the city416. Therefore, there were always several dozen of them, both in the city and in the suburbs. After 1772, their role was taken over by inns, of which there were 57 in 1807, with 31 in the city. Christians operated 49 of them, while only 8 were run by Jews417.

From the moment of its foundation, Zamość was intended to be the centre of the estates of its founder, initially only the Zamość estate. It began to fulfill this function in the autumn of 1586 when in a letter written from Belz on 21 November, the chancellor issued an order to the scribe Jan Piwko, instructing him to command the servant Wincenty “to keep castle always occupied”, and also ordering that Wincenty and another servant Miernicki should always spend the night there418. Wincenty and Miernicki were responsible for the supervision of Zamoyski’s new residence. The ordynats were obliged to take care of the city buildings and constantly modernize them420. Therefore, this city and fortress served as the main residence of the ordynats, where they received distinguished individuals, including ecclesiastical dignitaries, such as Patriarch Jeremiah II Tranos from Constantinople, whom Zamoyski invited in 1588421. Zamość was visited by many kings of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth: the Vasa kings, Michał Korybut Wiśniowiecki, Jan III Sobieski, August II, but also foreign monarchs, such as Swedish King Charles XII, and Tsar Peter I. The Zamoyski castle served as the main residence of the Zamoyski family and the capital of Ordynacja until 1806, when Stanisław Kostka Zamoyski, the 12th ordynat, moved the residence to Klemensów and the administration of the entail to Zwierzyniec422.

Jan Zamoyski, while constructing the city and residence, decided to surround them with modern bastion fortifications to provide defense against the frequent Tatar invasions plaguing Poland in the 16th c. The founder’s predictions proved to be correct. During the invasions of the late 16th and early 17th c., the Tatars bypassed this region423. The modern fortress became crucial in 1648 when Cossack-Tatar forces, after abandoning the siege of Lviv, began their march northward through the Commonwealth. The two-week defense of Zamość was effective, although it revealed many shortcomings in its preparation424. The role of the fortress and its defenders is better evaluated by military historians for the actions during the siege by the Swedish forces of King Charles X Gustav from 25 February to 1 March 1656, preceded by intensive preparations lasting from November 1655. The experiences of the two previous sieges prompted the ordynat Jan II Zamoyski to issue a proclamation “Warning for the Siege” in April 1657. Its intention was to better prepare the fortress and the city for the expected attack by Swedish or Transylvanian troops. The ordynat ordered the townspeople to gather supplies of grain and salted meat for a six-month period and to procure ammunition and gunpowder. The inhabitants of Zamość who could not prepare supplies were instructed to leave. Importing horses was prohibited. Water tanks were to be filled, and soaked skins were to be gathered for extinguishing fires. Guard posts were to be designated for this purpose. A register of residents who would participate in the defense and those preparing meals for soldiers was to be delivered to the castle. The city gates were to be closed, and only individuals with permission from the ordynat’s court could pass through them in both directions. Meetings and gatherings in the city, as well as contact with potential adversaries, were prohibited. Proof of such contacts would be considered treason, and in such a case, “such a one, with all his family and 419 Volumina constitutionum, vol. 2: 1587–1609, prep. for printing 420 Statuta Ordynacji Zamojskiej od r. 1589–1848, Warszawa 1902, household, may be forced to pay with his life and property”425. These regulations were subsequently treated as rules in case of danger.

The fame of the Zamość fortress during this period, enjoying the reputation of being impregnable, encouraged the nobility from the surrounding areas and from the southeastern regions to deposit their valuables there and to protect their families from dangers. Throughout the second half of the 17th c., the castle housed the municipal and county records of the Chełm Land. After the loss of Kamieniec Podolski in 1672, captured by the Turks, Zamość became the most important fortress in this part of the Commonwealth426. During disputes over the entail following the childless death of Jan II Zamoyski, one of the contenders – Marcin Zamoyski, the Lviv deputy pantler from a collateral branch of the family – took advantage of this situation. During the parliamentary debates on 29 January 1674, when accusations were made that the entail did not benefit the Commonwealth, Marcin Zamoyski made a declaration. He pledged to raise a unit of 200 dragoons for the defense of the country and to ensure the proper combat readiness of the Zamość fortress. When the vote was taken, the deputies supported the proposal to entrust the entail to him427. Bearing this in mind, the nobility from Belz and Chełm assembled near Zamość on 5 August 1675 and sent a petition to the King-elect Jan III Sobieski, urging him to send a contingent of royal troops as garrison for the fortress. In response, Sobieski wrote to the new ordynat, instructing him to deploy the promised unit of 200 dragoons to the fortress428. The consequence of these events was the enactment of the constitution during the coronation sejm of 1676 titled “The Zamość Fortress”. To Zamoyski’s declaration of maintaining the fortress in proper combat readiness, an obligation was added for the Commonwealth to equip it with artillery and ammunition429. To ensure the provision of food for the garrison, it was ordered that a warehouse would be established, to which all subjects of the entail were obliged to deliver half a bushel of Zamość measure of rye annually, “until the Turkish war is pacified”430. In the following years, the garrison of the Zamość fortress was granted equal rights with the komput army (a supplemental unit, financed with the komput, an army budged voted for by the Sejm). Appointed by the Grand Hetman of the Crown, the commanding officer held the rank of colonel, while their deputy held the rank of major431. All sides involved in the Northern War sought to seize the fortress, but it was successfully captured by the Saxons in December 1715. They only left Zamość in July of the following year432. The service in the fortress was resumed by the dragoons and riflemen enlisted by the ordynat. Their numbers fluctuated throughout the 18th c. In 1772, Zamość was occupied by the Austrians. Their garrison entered the city along with a large group of officials from the precinct and district. The ordynat’s buildings and citizens’ houses were taken over for the purposes of new officials and offices. The garrison was housed in buildings near the abandoned Armenian church, while warehouses and lazarets were established in several other former churches and monasteries, as well as in private houses. The occupiers considered themselves owners of the fortifications but did not carry out any renovations434. The combat value of the fortress diminished over time435. It was only the outbreak of the war with France and the Duchy of Warsaw that drew attention of the occupiers to Zamość, which was chosen as one of the locations for supply depots for the troops operating in the Duchy. Repair works were carried out hastily in order to make it in time before the approach of Polish forces in May 1809. After a nighttime attack on 19–20 May, the fortress was captured436. As already mentioned, a few weeks later, work began on the expansion of the fortress. The plan was drawn up by Colonel J. Mallet, commander of the engineering forces of the Duchy of Warsaw. The implementation was led by a major, and later by a lieutenant colonel, L. Jodko. Damage from the night assault was repaired and the first attempts at modernizing the fortifications were undertaken. These were completed in January 1813. The combat capability of the fortress was significantly increased. After 1809, Zamość also became a place where military units were formed. During preparations for the war with Russia, according to Emperor Napoleon’s plans, the Zamość fortress was to shield the march of the right wing of the grand army from the south, and for this purpose, reserves of ammunition and food for a three-month siege were to be prepared there. In 1813, it turned out that the defense lasted half a year longer and the fortress was not taken by the Russians, but surrendered by its defenders437. In the following years, a thorough reconstruction and modernization of the fortress were undertaken, also under the direction of Colonel J. Mallet438. Since then, it was the military function that began to dominate in the functional program of Zamość.

Kochnowski, the auxiliary bishop of Chełm, to this position, who already had similar powers previously granted by the ordinary bishop of Chełm445. The Uniate deanery was also included in the Przemyśl Uniate diocese446. After 1809, the affiliation of both deaneries returned to the situation before 1772, although the Catholic one, after the transfer of the Chełm diocese to Lublin and the establishment of the Lublin diocese in 1805, was incorporated into it447.

Cathedral, until 1992 collegiate church, of the Resurrection of the lord and St. Thomas is one of the most magnificent temples in Polish early modern architecture. It was built according to the design by Bernard Morando between 1587 and 1598448. It stands on two blocks in the southwest 439 A. Gil, Chełmska diecezja unicka 1596–1810. Dzieje i organizacja, Lublin 2005, p. 301. 440 Ibidem, p. 55. 441 A. Kossowski, Z dziejów zakonu bazylianów w Zamościu, “Teka 442 A. Gil, Chełmska diecezja unicka (as n. 439), p. 213. 443 J. Kowalczyk, Kolegiata (as n. 217), p. 21, 25, n. 39. 444 B. Kumor, Wydział teologiczny Akademii Zamojskiej (1648–1784), 445 Ibidem, p. 71. 446 A. Gil, Chełmska diecezja unicka (as n. 439), p. 119. 447 Ibidem, p. 180–181; F. Stopniak, Dzieje kapituły (as n. 217), part of the urban area, between the castle and the city449. It is a three-aisled church. The interior works were not completed before the death of the designer and architect (in 1600) and the founder (in 1605), so they extended over several more decades. On 5 December 1594, Pope Clement VIII in a bull approved the establishment of the collegiate church and established a chapter450. Six years later, on 5 July 1600, Jan Zamoyski issued the founding document for the church and the chapter. In the same year, services were transferred to it from the temporary Parish Church of St. Cross in the Lwowskie Suburb. Its parish priest, Father Stanisław Krassowski, relinquished the rich endowment of his provostship to the appointed prelate, also the parish priest of the collegiate church, Father Mikołaj Kiślicki, at the behest of Zamoyski451. After 1605, work on the interior decoration of the church progressed very slowly. It gained momentum in 1618 when Thomas, the son of the founder, reached adulthood and assumed the ordination. The finishing touches and the decorative network on the vaults of the aisles and chapels of the collegiate church were completed. The church received rich furnishings crafted by the best artisans from within the country and abroad. The solemn consecration of the collegiate church took place on 18 November 1637452. The interior was later enriched by the third ordynat, Jan II Zamoyski (1647–1665). On 18 April 1658, the church was hit by a massive fire. The roof, along with the small tower and spire, as well as the free-standing bell tower with bells and important buildings including the archives, were all consumed by the flames. However, the fire did not reach the interior of the church. The ordynat, the nobility and the municipal community participated in the reconstruction costs. The city community financed the reconstruction of the wooden bell tower in 1661, and in 1671, a new small tower was built on its roof, and a new spire was installed. Presumably, during this time, a porch was added to the facade453. The longstanding efforts of the chapter, in line with the recommendations of the bishops of Chełm, to build a brick bell tower were finally realized in the years 1760–1776 according to the design by Jerzy de Kawe454. Earlier, between 1731 and 1733, the collegiate church was renovated, while between 1773 and 1775, a monumental Baroque main altar was funded for it, which still exists to this day455. During the sieges in 1809 and 1813, the collegiate church was also damaged. Its emergency repairs in 1814 cost the chapter 2,000 złotys456; a general renovation was carried out in 1818457.

Church of the annunciation of the blessed Virgin mary was built between 1637 and 1662 for the Franciscans, who resided near the Church of the Holy Cross in the Lwowskie Suburb until 1655. The permission for them to build the church was issued by T. Zamoyski on 18 February 1636, and on 13 June 1637, 449 W. Kalinowski, Miasta polskie (as n. 122), p. 189. 450 J. The church is one of the most outstanding and largest Baroque religious buildings in Poland, surpassing even the collegiate church in size459. In 1642, the ordynat issued a permit, renewed in 1646, for the purchase of plots owned by townspeople on the southern side of the church under construction, where a Franciscan monastery was to be built460. In 1655, Bishop of Chełm Mikołaj Świrski consecrated the church and the two-story monastery with tiled roofs, whose expansion was completed in 1687461. The decoration work on the church continued until 1662. It was twice devastated by fires, in 1672 and 1709. After the second fire, around 1720, a freestanding bell tower was erected near the monastery, to the southwest of the church462. After the dissolution of the monastery and takeover of its assets by the Austrians in 1784, the Franciscan monks moved to the monastery of the Poor Clares. The Franciscans returned to their former premises in 1787, joining the Daughters of Charity brought from Lviv who already resided there, caring for sick soldiers463. In June 1809, the Franciscans received orders to leave the city. They moved to Górecko, taking several paintings and other items with them; the rich furnishings of their church were transferred to the collegiate church and other temples in the area. The church was converted into a warehouse for straw, hay, and from 1819, artillery equipment. It was rebuilt in 1821464.

Church of St. Nicholas was originally a wooden church built after 1589 by a community of Greek merchants in the southeast corner of the city, near Bastion I. Jan Zamoyski granted permission for its construction in a privilege dated 10 January 1589, which was confirmed in 1618 by T. Zamoyski465. In the early 17th c., an Orthodox Brotherhood of the Mother of God Protection began operating at this church. Between 1618 and 1631, a wooden structure was replaced by a masonry church, designed and built by Jan Jaroszewicz and Jan Wolf, funded by T. Zamoyski. This is one of the most beautiful churches in the city, combining elements of Latin architecture with a plan reminiscent of Moldavian churches466. After the departure of the Greeks from Zamość, it became an Orthodox church, which in 1699 joined the Union of Brest467. In the following year, the Basilian monks settled there, who received a privilege from Anna Zamoyska of Gnińscy in 1706 and resided in the convent adjacent to this church468. A tower with embrasure, designed by Jan M. Link, was added between 1690 and 1699469. Between 1757 458 APL, BOZ (as n. 139), ref. no. 1497, p. 1–4 (copy from 19th c.); S. Church of the holy Cross (I) was built in the Lwowskie Suburb as the first Catholic church. It was constructed between 1579 and 1583, although it was consecrated on 16 April 1581471. In 1582, a house for priests was built next to it, and on 25 March 1583 in Sielce, the chancellor appointed Father Stanisław Krassowski as the commander of this church, along with a second priest, a servant, and a cook472. Then, on 20 August 1584 in Lublin, Zamoyski issued a founding act of the temporary parish at this church, but he announced the construction of a church in the city, which would be its seat. The provost – and Father Krassowski – received a very rich endowment from a donation by Father Szymon ługowski; from it, he was to support four mansionaries. After the construction of the city church, this endowment was transferred to it473. After the foundation of the collegiate church on 5 July 1600, Krassowski relinquished his income in favor of Mikołaj Kiślicki, appointed as the provost of the collegiate chapter (see above). In 1603, the Church of the Holy Cross was handed over to the Franciscans, who henceforth conducted pastoral activities there, even after the construction of a church and monastery designated for them in the city474. The Church of the Holy Cross was burned down in 1648. It was rebuilt before 3 May 1667, when the first service was held475. Burned again in 1703 before the arrival of the Swedes, it was rebuilt the following year. It served as a hospital church until it was replaced by the Church of Our Lady of Loreto in 1714. In a dispute between the collegiate chapter and the Franciscans in 1780 over its ownership, the Bishop of Chełm ruled that it belonged to the collegiate chapter, but it would still be maintained by the Franciscans. It was burned down during the events of either 1809 or 1813 and was not rebuilt thereafter476. Church of St. Catherine was erected in the Lubelskie Suburb around 1620 by Katarzyna of Ostrogski family, the wife of T. Zamoyski. It was burned down before the siege of 1648477, and rebuilt before 1696, as it was listed in the city’s extent at that time478. During the burning of the suburbs in early 1703, it was burned again. In 1707, in the city extent, a “ground where the Church of St. Catherine was” was noted, and in 1709, in

the next extent, “Church of St. Catherine” was recorded479, indicating that it had been rebuilt. It probably was only rebuilt in 1714 when it was described that the church had a dome, along with the rectory and shelter, attributing its foundation to Father Gruszecki. During Austrian times, it was liquidated. It was dismantled in the autumn of 1793. From 1793 to 1795, the new brick church in the shape of a rotunda started to be build on this site, funded by the citizens and clergy, supported by Konstancja of Czartoryski family Zamoyska, the widow of ordynat Andrzej. The new structure was designed by the architect Ferdinand Merksen. The first service was held there in November 1795. This church was mainly intended for Austrian soldiers. In 1810, it was dismantled, and the furnishings were transferred to other churches480. Church of St. anne. In Zamość, from the mid-17th c., there was a female community belonging to the Third Order of Franciscans, known as Tertiaries. They had their house and chapel on the then Ślusarska Street, near the Franciscan church. In 1676, it transformed into a cloistered convent after Sister Katarzyna Zielińska arrived from Stary Sącz. She persuaded seven sisters living in Zamość to adopt the Second Rule of the religious order and became their first prioress481. The new convent and church were built near the Water Market, occupying five plots of land purchased from the citizens482. The masonry church was erected around 1696, funded by Anna Zamoyska, the widow of the ordynat Marcin, according to the design by Jan M. Link483. The masonry monastery was built between 1757 and 1769, probably according to the design by the architect Jerzy de Kawe, funded by Jan Jakub Zamoyski484, one of the guardians of the minor Klemens Jerzy, the ordynat between 1760 and 1767, and then his successor. Work on this building lasted until 1775485. On 3 February 1782, the Poor Clares were forced to leave Zamość. In 1788, their buildings were taken over by the Grey Sisters, who established a hospital operating until 1812, when the church and monastery were taken over by the military and converted into a military hospital486.

Church of the assumption of the blessed Virgin mary mother of god was an Armenian church built in the eastern part of the city, outside the quadrangle of its buildings. Its facade closed off Armenian Street. The rectory and auxiliary buildings were erected on the southern side492. The construction of the wooden church along with the bell tower was overseen by Father łukasz, who arrived from Lviv. He entrusted the pastoral work to Father Krzysztof Kałast493. From 1623, Armenians, led by Father Jakub Ałtunowicz and the merchant Warteres Kirkorowicz, raised funds for the construction of a masonry church. The solemn laying of the cornerstone took place on 25 May 1626, with the participation of dignitaries of the Armenian Church. The church was dedicated to the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary the Mother of God. Bricks for the construction were fired in a brickyard established on land granted to the Armenians outside the city walls494. The construction work was completed in 1633. It was a small single-nave church with a transept and an east-facing chancel. The octagonal bell tower was built next to it, on the southern side. The consecration of the church took place on 14 September 1645, officiated by Father Jędrzej, the Bishop of Bogdania (Moldavia). Notably absent were dignitaries of the Armenian Church from Lviv, who had been in union with the Roman Catholic Church since 1630. The Armenians of Zamość were initially reluctant to join the union but eventually did so in 1665 after repeated persuasions495. The church was richly furnished thanks to the generosity of the local Armenians. Nevertheless, in a fire on 8–9 June 1672, the bell tower was destroyed. The flames “melted two large bells, and two smaller ones, causing significant damage and cracks in the church vaults”. The priests’ houses and five tenements, donated 488 J. The church and its premises were rebuilt, but it took several years to complete due to difficulties in trade with the East during the wars with Turkey, which impoverished the Armenians. Additionally, many Armenians began to leave Zamość during this time497. Once again, the church was engulfed by fire during a blaze that broke out in that part of the city on 4 October 1709. The roof and dome of the church were consumed by flames, as well as the roof structure of the bell tower, although the bells were spared. The vaults were secured against the autumn rains. However, because the fundraising efforts for the reconstruction yielded little result, as “the nation has diminished in wealth, and the help for the church restoration is not sufficient”, the parish assembly instructed Father Derbedrosowicz to seek permission from the Archbishop of Lviv for the sale of some church silverware. The money from the sale were earmarked for the church’s reconstruction. Such permission was obtained498. The repair of the roof, dome, and bell tower was carried out in 1710499. The church remained under the care of Armenian priests even after the suspension of the Armenian community’s activities. Due to its poor condition, the Austrian authorities ordered its dissolution in 1802. The furnishings were transferred to neighboring Catholic churches, and the building was put up for auction, which was won by the ordynat Stanisław Kostka, who then donated it to the city. Initially, the fortress command intended to use it as a warehouse, but this plan was abandoned, and the building was demolished between 1826 and 1827. Its foundations were discovered during the construction of the “Renaissance” hotel500. Church of the holy Cross (II) at the monastery of Brothers Hospitallers of Saint John of God. Its foundation took place in 1657 at the initiative of Bishop Mikołaj Świrski, the suffragan bishop of Chełm. Rector Rudomicz wrote in his diary that on 27 April 1657, “the erection of the hospital began”, but he added that five days earlier he had hosted, among others, the superior of the Brothers501. We do not know whether it was a freestanding building or connected to the hospital and monks’ quarters502. The wooden convent buildings burned down during the city fire on 8 June 1672503. As recorded in the property extents of 1696, 1707 and 1709, they were rebuilt504. The fire of 4 October 1709 once again affected

In 1714, the dean and protonotary Wawrzyniec Sikorski founded a provostship for two hospitals in Zamość, which were previously supervised by protonotaries. The provostship was established in 1715 by Father Walenty Konstanty Czubski, archdeacon and judicial vicar of Chełm. The provost’s house was erected opposite the Church of the Holy Cross in the Lwowskie Suburb. The church was built in 1717 by Father Tomasz Olszówka, who took the position of provost509. It served as a hospital church until the 1780s when it was “inclined to collapse”, meaning it required renovation. At that time, the provost, Father Stanisław Dąbkowski, had no money for this due to the Austrians taking away all the endowments. With the help of Jan Jakub Zamoyski, a new church was erected between 1780 and 1782. Ordynacja and the citizens supported the investment with building materials. Its cost was estimated at 2,342 złotys in 1781. These funds proved to be short of 600 złotys, which were, however, obtained anyway, and the construction was completed the following year510. However, it did not serve the residents and the faithful for long, as around 1795 it was demolished, and the bricks from its foundations were used in 1796 to build the fence around the Church of St. Catherine511.

Orthodox Church of the ascension of Christ was built of wood in the Lwowskie Suburb after the founding of the city, on the northern side of the Lviv road, near the Church of the Holy Cross. It was recorded in the extent of 1591512. The clergy and parishioners of this church joined the Union of Brest. We know little about its fate in the 17th c. Only from 1689 do we have information about admonitions from the Bishop of Chełm, Aleksander Augustyn łodziata, to the parishioners and members of the brotherhood associated with the church. Synagogue was built between 1610 and 1620 in the late Renaissance style, on the site of a wooden church from the late 16th c., at the corner of Żydowska Street and the fourth cross street (now Bazyliańska Street). In the 1630s, two lower narthexes were added on the north and south sides519. To the west, it adjoined two houses of the Jewish community, with the first serving as a Jewish school520. The synagogue underwent several reconstructions. It was destroyed by the Germans during the occupation from 1939 to 1944. Currently, it has been rebuilt and is under the care of the Foundation for the Preservation of Jewish Heritage in Warsaw521. The hospital at the Church of the holy Cross in the Lwowskie Suburb was founded after the parish foundation, in 1586. Walenty the carpenter erected a wooden building consisting of two rooms, designated for men and women522. In 1591, Jan Zamoyski supported the this hospital with a sum of 100 red złotys523. After his death, the management of Ordynacja contributed to the maintenance of this facility; for instance, in 1607, they allocated 114 złotys524. The fate of this hospital during the 17th c. remains unknown; it is possible that it was burned during the destruction of the suburbs in 1648 and 1657, but later it was rebuilt. It was recorded in the city’s extents of 1696 and 1707526. The lack of mention of it in the 1709 extent may be due to oversight, as it was functioning in 1714 when a prebend was established for the hospitals under the jurisdiction of the collegiate chapter527. The new hospital building was erected in 1721. Collegiate visitations from 1765 and 1770 describe it, although its condition was assessed as very poor. The collegiate chapter appealed to the ordynat for the hospital’s reconstruction. Initially, plans were made for a stone building, but a wooden one was erected in 1774–1775 instead. The founder appealed to Pope Clement VIII for permission to establish the Academy and the associated collegiate church. On 29 October 1594, the Pope issued the bull Sedes Apostolica, by the power of which he erected the Canonical Studium generale – referred to as the University of Zamość – with three faculties. The Chancellor’s intention was to establish a higher school distinct from the Cracow and Vilnius Academies. It was envisioned as a school of civic education, preparing young nobles for future public life and duties within the state. Additionally, it was expected to engage in creative work in popular scientific fields such as classical philology and history, aiming to become the main conduit of Polish scientific thought with the West591. The official opening ceremony of the Academy took place on 15 March 1595. To commemorate this event, the founder issued a “Appeal to the Polish people”, praising education and encouraging studying. He also presented the ideological program of the university592. In July of the same year, the Chancellor, together with the Bishop of Chełm, approved the university’s statute593. Zamoyski issued two founding acts – for the academy and collegiate church. Education at the Academy was to be conducted at two levels: lower, five-year level, and higher, sixyear level. These acts marked the beginning of the 184-year history of the university, during which it experienced periods of successful development (the most successful being the first decade), as well as less favorable times – lack of financial resources, significant economic dependence on church authorities, a decline in the quality of teaching, and limited progress in scientific research. Even before the inauguration of the university in March 1594, a complex of buildings was constructed for it in the northwest part of the urban area, referred to by T. Zarębska forty-five years ago as the “university town”. The first building had five lecture halls and nine rooms. It was depicted in Braun’s view598. In the literature to date, it is generally accepted that the current quadrangle of the Academy with a square courtyard in the middle replaced the original building, which was situated in the place of subsequent western wing, but burned down during the fire of 1633599. In the spring of 1639, the widow of Tomasz Zamoyski, Katarzyna of Ostrogski family, commenced the construction of a new building, according to the design by Bernard Morando – or perhaps by Andrzej dell’Aqua or Jan Jaroszewicz. On 27 August, Dean Jakub Skwarski consecrated the building600. It was being erected until 1648, and complementary finishing works continued in the following years. It underwent multiple reconstructions601. Repairs and renovations were also carried out in the first half of the 18th c.602. The Austrian rule worsened the already precarious financial situation of the Academy. It was cut off from revenues from estates and sums invested in various properties of the Commonwealth due to the border, and the Austrian authorities taxed the subjects in the village of Bukowina, which belonged to the Academy. As a result, the inhabitants there continued to fall behind in paying the rents owed to the Academy, and part of the premises in the building was occupied by the army603. From 1780 onwards, rumors began to spread that the Austrians, as part of their educational reforms in the annexed territories, intended to close down the Academy. The Bishop of Przemyśl informed the rector on 15 October 1783, that future priests would henceforth be educated in Lviv, which meant the closure of the theological seminary associated with the university. Sawa, Akademia Zamojska (as n. 598), p. 95–96. On the night of 19 May 1809, the Polish forces led by Prince Józef Poniatowski besieged Zamość and captured the city. As a result, Zamość, along with its surrounding district (administrative division of the Habsburg monarchy), was incorporated into the Duchy of Warsaw under the protection of Napoleon.

After Napoleon’s defeat and the Congress of Vienna (1815), Zamość and its surroundings were incorporated into the Kingdom of Poland, which was subordinated to the Russian Empire. The strategically located fortress was predisposed to protect Russia’s borders against potential enemies, particularly the Austrian Empire. Consequently, the Zamoyski family decided to sell their ancestral city to the government of the Kingdom. At the end of 1815, at the request of the ordynat, Tsar Alexander I established a new commission with the fortress commander, General Józef Wasilewski, chosen as its president. In 1816, the commission designated the second strategic perimeter, the Border of the Fortress Region, located at the distance of a powerful cannon shot, estimated at 2339 meters from the fortifications609. 609 In 1816, the planning and development of the suburban areas began from scratch based on three strategic perimeters. The first of these was the Border of the Fortress, encompassing the defensive works system and their surroundings, forming the so-called pochodzistość forteczną. Another one, the first strategic perimeter – The Total Construction Prohibition Border, established after the siege in 1809 as a buffer zone of the fortress, intended for the planned expansion of the outer defensive earthworks. This zone was to remain without any construction within a distance of 600 Russian fathoms (approximately 1,169 meters) from the fortress’s glacis. The buildings were to be assessed and relocated beyond the outer boundary line, as they could hinder the fortress’s defence during a siege. In March 1816, at the request of the entailer, Tsar Alexander I appointed the Regulatory Commission, which designated the first strategic perimeter – the Border of the Fortress Region, estimated at 600–1200 Russian fathoms (approximately 1,169–2,139 meters) from the glacis. The demarcation of this zone was carried out by Colonel Leonard Jodko, at the command of General Józef Wasilewski. Within this perimeter, there were 3,271 morgens of land, of which 999 belonged to burghers, while the Zamoyski Entail owned 2,105 morgens. Many of these lands belonged to the Żdanów, Mokre, Janowice, Płoskie, and Kalinowice granges. Before finalising the sale transaction of Zamość, the perimeter’s area was adjusted concerning the planned defensive works. Within the second strategic perimeter, property owners whose buildings were burned during sieges or demolished during fortification construction were relocated. The institution of Zamość Fortress Engineering Directorate, which operated from 1820–1827, continued modernising the fortifications610. The demolition of the remnants of suburbs and buildings in nearby villages began in the spring of 1824. Five new settlements with simple urban layouts and characteristics of villages or small cities were planned within the scope of the second strategic perimeter. These suburbs were supposed to take over the previous civic functions of Zamość. Ultimately, apart from the Nowa Osada Suburb, the realisation of other suburbs could not be achieved611. In 1818, as a result of the reform of self-government administration in the Kingdom of Congress Poland, the offices of city council were replaced by the supervisory bodies for towns and cities. ; Upon a decree of the Viceroy from 30 May 1818 the Municipal Offices led by a mayor were established. In 1827, after the nationalisation of Zamość, the Municipal Office aimed to elevate the mayor to a president status due to additional responsibilities associated with the dynamics of spatial and population changes. The lay judges took over some of the mayor’s competencies. Conflicts arose between the municipal authorities and the military command over compensations for the citizens’ properties destroyed due to the fortification expansion612. Due to the fortress expansion, services and some public functions were relocated to the newly established suburb called Nowa Osada, situated along the Lviv route. Until the fall of the November Uprising, the mayor’s office and the Municipal Of- tlers were apprehensive about the proximity to the fortress in case of a war outbreak. The process of relocating properties was lengthy due to the slow pace of compensation payments and the allocation of plots within the second strategic perimeter. Z. The fortress perimeter was reinforced by constructing a cavalier (zaszaniec, properly ziemny nadszaniec) in the gorges of the bastions nos. 4, 6, and 7. The flanks of bastion no. 5 and the left flank of bastion no. 6 were enclosed, creating a wide gorge of the bastion with a casemate and a passageway through the postern in the orillon. By 1813, the ravelin in front of curtain wall VI-VII and the slopes serving as a breastwork for the covertway had yet to be completed. At Napoleon’s request, the fortress protected the right wing of the Grande Armée marching towards Moscow627. During the winter of 1812/1813, as the retreating French forces left, the Russians entered the territory of the Duchy. This led to the siege of the Zamość fortress, which began on 22 January 1813. General Maurycy Hauke628 began gathering food, animal and ammunition supplies. Two military defensive lines were established around the fortress. On 24 February, Russian forces commanded by General Simeon L. Rath pushed the Poles out of Lublin area and blockaded the Zamość fortress. Zamość could not rely on supplies from outside. Despite the hardships, the siege was endured for nine months. Worsening supply, sanitary conditions, and high soldier mortality led to the surrender of Zamość. After the terms of surrender were established on 25 November, the garrison left the fortress with full honours and went into captivity629. Only the better-equipped Modlin fortress was defended longer than Zamość. Tsar Alexander I of Russia was impressed by the monthslong defence of Zamość. Thus, he insisted on expediting the sale of the city. The decision to sell the estate to which every ordynat was emotionally attached was slowly becoming evident to the Zamoyski family630. The fortress was planned to be modernised in accordance with plans of General Ignacy Prądzyński. The altered defence strategy of the Kingdom of Poland pointed to the most significant threat coming from Prussia and Austria. Significant investments were directed towards fortifying the country’s northern territories, but as for the Austrian border, the modernisation of Zamość was advocated631. The task was entrusted to Lieutenant Colonel Leonard Jodko, assisted by Captains Bernard Engbricht and Aleksander Linsenbarth632.

Before Zamość was sold to the government, the ramparts were strengthened by vaulted shooting galleries within the former scarps connecting the bastion casemates. The base of the ramparts and the rampart road were widened, while the entrances to the casemates, posterns and underground corridors were expanded. Bastions were widened by vaulting the recessed flanks, creating large casemates for prison and gunpowder storage635. On the fronts of curtain walls IV-V, V-VI, VII-I, and I-II, a Carnot wall was constructed, which was additionally enclosed in the corners, equipped with embrasures and a cunette scarp. The basis for it was the 17-century earthen rampart, which in 1809–1813, disappeared from the fortress’ foreground due to advances in military tactics. The Carnot wall stood at a height of 2.7 meters and had a thickness ranging from 0.8 to 1.2 meters. It followed a continuous zigzag line along the axis of the curtain walls and in front of the bastion salient636. It was lower than the dry moat level , running above the water ditch. At the end of the wall line were sluices for regulating the water level in the moat. They were positioned along the axis of curtain wall IV-V and in front of the right face of bastion no. 1. Casemated guardrooms were established at the bends of the wall in front of the bastion angles637. The next stage of thorough changes to the fortress included the construction of two new gates. During the Duchy of Warsaw period, ordynat Stanisław Kostka Zamoyski and the citizens of Zamość appealed to the King of Saxony and the Duke of Warsaw, Frederick Augustus, for a compensation for the damaged property654. Since 1811, commissions began their work, estimating the value of buildings occupied by the military and considering claims from civilians. Frederick Augustus confirmed his will that the government take over the management of the Zamość fortress along with its surroundings in exchange for national assets655. At the end of 1815, at the request of Zamoyski, Tsar Alexander I established a new commission, which in 1816 designated the second strategic perimeter – the Border of the Fortress Region at a distance of “a powerful cannon shot”, i.e., 2339 meters from the fortifications. Negotiations were conducted between the Tsar and the ordynat, resulting in an agreement on 4 August 1818, to exchange Zamość for national assets: Kołodziąż in the Podlaskie province and Jadów in the Masovian province. However, these properties did not have sufficient value, so additional properties, Wiski and Planta from the Podlaskie province, were included. The final settlement and the drafting of the definitive agreement for the exchange or sale of Zamość to the government of the Kingdom of Poland occurred on 14 August 1820. The Tsar approved the articles in the document, which empowered the Government Commission of Income and Treasury to finalise the perpetual transaction. The final contract was drawn up on 30 January 1821. The compensation for the properties and income of the city amounted to 3,426,171 zlotys and 11 grosze. The overall value of the national assets to be exchanged was estimated to be higher by 178,000 zlotys. As a result, the ordynat undertook to pay this additional value to the State Treasury in equal instalments spread over six years656.

During the period of the Duchy of Warsaw and the Kingdom of Poland, the civil structure of Zamość withered away. The representative space of the Great Market was fragmented, following a disruption of the property structure caused by the introduction of the military substance. The army occupied the Lord’s Tenement and the city hall. The civilian authority located in the city hall was brutally pushed out by the military authority, which sought dominance over the city. The buildings of the former Poor Clares’ nunnery were converted into barracks, a lazaretto, and storage facilities. In 1820, the church of St. Anne underwent reconstruction, whereas the convent’s reconstruction did not start until 1850. The Water Market was shifted towards the east, acquiring a rectangular shape of 50 x 70 meters661. Three buildings in the eastern frontage were demolished. After Zamość was sold to the government, investments were directed towards enhancing the linear fortifications and point installations662. Prisoners settled within the fortress were ordered to do the labour. Bastion no. 5 underwent repairs, while bastion no. 6 was expanded. The ramparts were reinforced, and preparations were undertaken to construct the Nowa Lubelska Gate. A shooting gallery comprising 18 casemates was established within the curtain wall V-VI. By 1821, the curtain wall VIVII had undergone reconstruction, creating a shooting gallery featuring 38 casemates, an underground communication network and 44 firing positions. In 1821–1825, the Szczebrzeska Gate, initially in the Rococo style, underwent a reconstruction in the Neoclassical style. This transformation involved the removal of the ornamental attic and sculptures of St. Florian and St. Michael the Archangel. The brick facades of the gate were made to resemble the appearance of the frontage of fortress curtain walls. A monogram of Emperor Alexander I was placed in the semicircle above the passage. Likely, the author of the gate reconstruction project was Jan Paweł Lelewel665. The facades were adorned with bossages in large pilaster strips and window frames. The guardhouse was situated on the ground floor; the casemates were used as prison cells, while the upper floor as the accommodations for officers666. A guardhouse in the form of a blockhouse was constructed on the ravelin by the Szczebrzeszyn route around 1825. Between 1822 and 1824, the postern in the curtain wall V-VI was replaced with the Nowa Lubelska Gate. This gate replaced the previous one located near bastion no. 5. The project was developed and supervised by Lieutenant Colonel Lelewel667. The building featured a monumental brick-and-stone facade, with stone-cut arch frame elements and the Doric frieze with triglyphs in the crowning. In the keystone above the passage arch, a bas-relief of oak branches symbolising martial courage was placed, along with the initials “AI” against a background of rays, signifying the Emperor of Russia and King of Poland, Alexander I. The lower side sections had more modest entrances leading to vaulted barrel-shaped prison casemates added in the mid-19th c. In 1824, the Nowa Lubelska Gate held 110 prisoners, overseen by officers who also resided in the Stara Lubelska Gate668, which was also converted into a prison casemate. The southern guardhouse was liquidated. From the city side, a casemated shelter was established within the curtain wall, extending to bastion no. 1669. The casemates housed the so-called correctional prison. The inner facade was devoid of a passage arch. In 1824, there were plans to construct a third masonry cavalier in the gorge of bastion no. 2, but they were not realised670. After 1821, a two-storey defensive traverse was built on the plateau of bastion no. 1 connected to the shooting gallery, completing the curtain wall VII-I671. In the vicinity of the fortifications, retrenchments were planned to support the defence of the prominent ravelins. A casemated retrenchment was successfully built in front of the eastern curtain wall VI-VII, aligned with the lunette in the foreground, which already had an internal retrenchment. This structure was established on the place-ofarms of the covertway. The purpose of the retrenchment was to provide firing support for the prominent lunette, and in the event of its capture, it was meant to serve as a protective barrier for curtain wall VI-VII672.

No substantial reserve barracks and auxiliary blockhouses (powder storage facility) were constructed within the fortification perimeter673. They were intended to be placed inside the couvrefaces of bastions nos. 3 and 4 and within the ravelin of curtain walls III-IV. The outer defensive works were enclosed by a shared slope with a sawtooth profile featuring place-ofarms and the covertway.
