A characteristic defensive element of the foreground became a brick cannon emplacement extended in the southern front of the fortress. It was built on Kempa Island in the area of Wielka Zalewa, in the place of the lunette in front of bastion no. 2 and the ruins of the fortalicium. The structure’s construction took place between 1825 and 1831, most likely according to the design by Lieutenant Colonel Jan Paweł Lelewel675. The structure was built on a ring-shaped layout with a diameter of 54 meters. The inner courtyard had a diameter of 38.5 meters and was open towards the fortress. The 9.4 meters in height walls were covered with a shingled roof, later replaced with an earthen roof. The facility consisted of 20 concentrically arranged casemated rooms of a radial shape, each having a depth of 6.2 meters and a width ranging from 3.5 to 5 meters. These rooms opened onto the courtyard through wide arches for artillery placement. Embrasures were placed in the outer wall, which was 2.6 meters thick676. The cannon emplacement was connected to the fortress by a defensive road, reinforced with three traverses of a rampart-like cross-section, positioned on its toothed widenings. These military works played a significant strategic role in guarding the access to the fortress from the south. Its prominent positioning on the foreground allowed it to command over the Żdanowska causeway, nearby elevations, and the opposite “Zamczysko” (castle) area677. In 1821–1825, the arsenal underwent modernisation according to the design by General Malletski. The three-arched gate was reconstructed with a triangular crown and a rusticated portico.The window frames were stripped off. The arsenal gained an additional floor covered by a hipped roof678. Drill grounds were organised within the fortress, with the largest in front of the Zamoyski Palace. Smaller drill grounds were arranged in the place of the demolished Reformed Franciscan monastery near the Salt Market679, adjacent to the orthodox church and Basilian monastery, and by the traverse of bastion no. 1. Similar functions were fulfilled by places near the gates, military structures, and certain bastion casemates. Drill ground also operated within the fortress’s foregrounds, including between curtain wall VI-VII and the lunette. From 1824 to 1829, due to the modernisation of Lubelska Street leading to the Nowa Lwowska Gate, the Zamość Fortress Engineering Directorate took over ten properties leased by the Municipal Office at the Salt Market to expand the drill ground near the former church of Reformed Franciscans.

Sroczyńska, Zamojska twierdza (as n. 610), p. 18. The Zamość fortress had a prison, which was the most severe penitentiary facility in the Kingdom of Poland. Political and military prisoners were held here and used for laborious fortress tasks680. In 1823, works began on a brick outbuilding for the prison at the Salt Market, according to the design by General Malletski. The building was situated parallel to the city hall, replacing the stalls for butchers and craftsmen and the headquarters of the City Weighhouse. The facility was distinguished by a monumental front gate adorned with a bas-relief of a lion’s head and symbols of justice681. Inside there were an officer and non-commissioned officer accommodations, a kitchen and rooms for military craftsmen. A rectangular courtyard with a brick-lined well was erected between the outbuilding and the city hall. During the Kingdom of Poland, there was a decline in the economic splendour of Zamość. Most traders and craftsmen left the city, and crafts were mainly concentrated at the stalls. The degradation of Zamość to the status of a small administrative capital deprived the struggling craftsmen and traders of the profits they used to receive from officials and their families, as well as from people visiting the city682. Some of the tenement owners at the Market closed shops, sold properties and, due to a lack of prospects, left Zamość. The arcades on the Market were walled up so that small traders could display their goods there, as they could not afford to rent spaces in the tenements. Jews opened shops and stalls in properties acquired from Armenians, Sephardic Jews, Germans, and Greeks683. The Zamość Fortress Engineering Directorate relocated the fairs outside the fortress area for safety reasons. The Government Commission of Income and Treasury objected to it, as it meant the loss of income. In August 1821, Grand Duke Konstantin decided that fairs be organized in the place by the Lviv route684, which became an indirect cause of another population decline within the fortress. Zamość was surpassed in terms of profitable fairs not only by Lublin, Chełm, and Krasnystaw but even by Turobin and Frampol685. Data shows that in 1821, there were 66 traders and 62 multi-purpose shops and stalls owned by Jews. The most common types of shops were those selling wine, textiles and clothing, spices, and leather goods. In 1822, on the order of Grand Duke Konstantin, the stalls were demolished, leaving several traders unemployed, who were also removed from the arcades of the city hall.

The calamity consumed 54 buildings and damaged 20 others. The process of consolidating plots partially obscured the original property divisions. The government took measures to acquire all private properties, appointing a commission to assess the civil structures’ worth. After 1821, there was a shift in the demand structure of craftsmanship. Tailors and shoemakers who made uniforms for the military, as well as craftsmen who supplied the garrison with food, were in demand. As compensation for the demolished slaughterhouses, authorities allowed butchers to sell products in the arcades by the city hall. Frequent renovations of military facilities and tenements attracted skilled masons and carpenters to the fortress. The state supervision and the allowing unaffiliated individuals to work in various specialties became the primary reasons behind the dissolution of guild organisations. Impoverished artisans practiced their craft with impunity. While there were ten guilds within the fortress, it was evident that craftsmen were increasingly relocating to the suburbs. In 1823, the military relocated the butchers to the arcades of the tenement houses; however, by 1830, the Zamość Fortress Engineering Directorate advocated for the construction of new slaughterhouses696. As part of the road system modernisation, the original Lwowska and Lubelska Gates were replaced by two new passageways along the axes of curtains. Adjustments were made in the foreground of the fortress area to refine the routes to Lviv and Lublin. Implementing these new gates necessitated a change in the communication route through the ramparts, Brukowana Street, the Great Market, and up to place-of-arms in front of the former Zamoyski Palace. Due to the bricking up of the Stara Lubelska Gate, the placeof-arms lost its role as the primary communication hub of the fortress. The southern part of this place, paved with stones, was overtaken by the route to Szczebrzeszyn, between the former Zamoyski Palace and the collegiate church. In 1823, it was planned to construct a military road along the southern ramparts, in order to connect the Szczebrzeska Gate with the plateau of bastion no. 2. This development involved requisitioning of the collegiate garden and the demolition of the postal stables near the gate. Following the opening of the Nowa LubelskaGate, the paving of Lubelska Street commenced. This thoroughfare facilitated communication between the city hall and the guardhouse, passing through the Salt Market and former Chełmska Street to the synagogue, from where it continued straight toward the entrance. To ensure the proper width of the road, a Jewish building on the Salt Market was demolished, and thirteen houses were earmarked for demolition697. In 1827, there were plans to extend Ogrodowa and Bazyliańska streets to the ramparts, and to direct Bazyliańska Street towards the curtain wall I-II, but the monastery situated tranversely made it impossible. Ogrodowa Street was extended eastward towards the place of the former Franciscan monastery. The perspective of this thoroughfare was closed off by the blockhouse of curtain wall VII-I. The modernisation of Zamość fortress brought about significant changes to its surrounding areas. The expansion of the outer defensive perimeter led to the transformation of the suburbs, which had already been functioning in a relic form since the siege of 1813. From 1820, the plans of the Zamość Fortress Engineering Directorate envisioned the creation of entirely new suburban settlements situated at a distance of at least 600 fathoms from the fortress walls. These settlements were intended to gradually take over the civil functions of intramural Zamość. The scope of these changes was presented in the fortress plans drawn up in the 1820s by General Jan Chrzciciel Malletski699 and Colonel Jan Paweł Lelewel700. Inventory and measurement work was conducted on the plots around the fortress, as the inhabitants of the suburbs had abandoned their buildings before 1821. In 1823, the army demarcated 666 plots around the fortress to provide affected residents with compensatory land on the new suburbs. Ultimately, the Regulatory Commission demarcated 442 plots due to the number of citizens who declared an interest. In the spring of 1824, the remnants of old suburban and village buildings were demolished. The undeveloped lands were repurposed for various uses, including pastures and a marketplace701. New settlement units were to be built within the area of the second strategic perimeter (600–1200 fathoms from the fortifications). Ultimately, instead of five, two suburbs were established along the main roads leading out of the fortress. The Nowa Osada Suburb, established 1.5 km southeast from the fortifucations along the Lviv route, quickly took on the city’s civil functions. Along the Lublin and Skierbieszów routes, the less-developed Lubelskie Suburb was created. These two units were connected by Obwodowa Street, which was laid out around 1823, bypassing the fortress from the northeast702.

Zamość developed in accordance with the paradigm aimed at breaking the compactness of its spatial structure. The suburbs, distant from one another, were prevented from merging into a single urban entity with the fortress703. Nowa Osada was laid out within the confines of the second strategic perimeter – 1.5 km from the Great Market. This suburb was planned on both sides of the newly established Lviv route, which served as the shorter symmetrical axis of the urban layout. The longer axis was defined by the new Hrubieszów route intersecting perpendicularly the Lviv route. At their crossing point, a place measuring 110 m × 150 m was marked out and named New Market (Nowy Rynek), serving as the centrepiece of Nowa Osada707. General Jan Chrzciciel Malletski designed this chequered layout of the suburb. Two diagonally running thoroughfares bounded the settlement, to the north and south: the new section of the Hrubieszów route and the old Lviv route, giving it a characteristic elongated trapezoidal shape. On both sides of the new Lviv route, 442 building plots were demarcated. The New Market’s frontages were wooden arcaded buildings typical of provincial towns. By the end of 1826, Nowa Osada counted 250 properties and 192 undeveloped plots708. During the November Uprising, 193 houses in Nowa Osada were razed, significantly impeding the suburb’s growth. By 1839, there were 200 undeveloped plots, further exacerbating the urban disorder of the settlement710. In 1854, Nowa Osada was home to 1,567 residents. By the end of 1865, there were 277 wooden and nine brick houses. In 1866, the erection of agricultural buildings and wooden houses near New Market was forbidden. Nowa Osada was connected to the Podtopole Grange, Kalinowice Ordynackie, and Wólka Miejska. The new Lubelskie Suburb, created with less splendour than Nowa Osada, was situated along the newly traced road to Lublin, approximately 1.5 km from the fortress’s Market, . The development of this unit progressed rather slowly. Until the outbreak of the November Uprising, the settlement remained largely undeveloped. The only exceptions were a few relic houses from the old suburb and Janowice village, which had been relocated to the left bank of the łabuńka River. In 1821, there were 45 houses. During the November Uprising, 76 buildings were destroyed, which made it challenging to establish a central area for the suburb in the following years. The focus of the settlement shifted along the road to Majdan, leading to the area’s designation in the mid-19th century as Lubelskie Suburb – Majdanek711. Following the November Uprising, General Ivan Döhn ordered the delineation of a third strategic perimeter around the fortress at a distance of 200 m, similar to the protective zones around the Modlin Fortress. Lands acquired by the military were partially designated for the military gardens, including the commandant’s orchard (sad komendancki) along the łabuńka River. In 1837, Wielka Zalewa was drained, and the course of the łabuńka River was redirected through the Podtopole Grange713. In September 1830, the fortress counted 4,652 soldiers from the staff of the 2nd Infantry Division commanded by General Edward Żółtowski, the 1st and 2nd Battalions of the 2nd and 4th Infantry Riflemen Regiments, which were part of the 3rd Infantry Riflemen Brigade, an Uhlans unit, two artillery squads, the 3rd Active Veterans Battalion, a logistics company, and a craftsmen company719. The history of Zamość is indelibly marked by its participation in the November Uprising of 1830–1831. It stood as one of the two fortresses in the Congress Kingdom alongside Modlin, surpassing the latter in terms of armament and fortification720. Colonel Jan Krysiński, an experienced officer who had served in the Legions and the Polish Army of the Duchy of Warsaw, then the Congress Poland, was appointed commander. Two staircases allowed access to the attic, where further firing devices were located. Behind the breastwork arranged there, cannons were positioned, raised via a ramp connecting the attic with the rampart road.

In the mid-1850s, Russia began dismantling outdated fortresses. General Engineer Eduard Ivanovich Todleben, the director of the Engineer Department of the Ministry of War, was in charge of this task. He developed plans to modernise the existing fortresses of the Russian Empire. Todleben rejected the doctrine of modernising fortress layouts according to the principles of the French school because such fortifications featured many concentrated masonry structures that were vulnerable to artillery fire. The invention of rifled artillery with extended range defined the direction of development of offensive tactics. The concentrated fortifications of Zamość, situated in open terrain, became a vulnerable target for elusive enemy artillery, which could operate beyond the scope of strategic perimeters. For this reason, Zamość was deemed unfit to be included among fortresses suitable for modernisation.746 After the fall of the January Uprising, the fate of Zamość was sealed. In the autumn of 1866, it was decided to dismantle the fortress. Military equipment and machinery were removed, the dismantling of fortifications began, and the command administration was dissolved. The fortress regiment was relocated to the expanding fortress of Ivanogorod747, while the garrison battalion was sent to the Warsaw Citadel. On 21 November 1866, in the decree the Tsar officially announced the abolition of the Zamość fortress as outdated and incompatible with modern military doctrine748. The collegiate church was renovated from 1824 to 1826 in the Neoclassical style. The church’s architectural design was aligned with the fortifications, downplaying its votive and triumphant character. During the renovation, the roofs above the chancel and naves were lowered. Above the front facade and the chancel opening, the gables were removed. In 1828, the bell tower was lowered, and its pinnacle was capped with a helmet-like structure devoid of the latticed lantern and tall spire it previously had. A major renovation oc-

The dismantling of the fortification allowed the creation of new roads through the demolished ramparts, enabling the free movement of people and goods between urban districts. The Lublin route (in the part of the Old Town) was given a Russified name, Lubelski Wyjazd (Lublin exit road). Its fundamental alignment toward the city hall tower remained essentially unchanged. However, instead of leading towards the Lubelska Nowa Gate, it led directly to the face of bastion no. 5, contributing to the blurring of its outline. The vast plateau of the military structure became an important transport hub of Zamość. Lubelski Wyjazd went slightly eastward, following the axis of a street leading to the Great Market. A new section of the street was laid along the western face of bastion no. 5, leading to Zamkowy (Castle) Square, which was transformed into Ordonanshauz Street in the early 20th c. This street served as the starting point for the road to Szczebrzeszyn. The road on the plateau of bastion no. 5 complemented a wide street from the east, a relic of the internal rampart road, providing communication between the Lublin and the Lviv routes. Following the fort’s dismantlement, this street became the main transit route through the city. Before World War I, the surface of the route was repaired823.

The narrow entrance to the city hindered communication. Officials advocated for demolishing the Lwowska Nowa Gate and its blockhouse, but the plans were not realised eventually824. In 1918, the former rampart road connecting Lviv exit road with Lublin exit road was renamed łukasińskiego Street. The road held importance for the transport in the city centre. Despite the existence of Obwodowa Street, the main transit route between Lublin and Lviv still passed through the city centre. The course of łukasińskiego Street ran alongside the fortifications and away from buildings, allowing for the appropriate road width. The northern section led through a market square by the Lubelska Nowa Gate. It was then routed through a meander between the gate and the northern cavalier, where there was a gap after the demolition of the curtain V-VI segment. In the 1880s, there were considerations to demolish the Lubelska Nowa Gate to straighten the course of łukasińskiego Street826. The road passed in front of the gate’s facade along the line of the former moat and connected with Lublin exit road on the plateau of bastion no. 5. The route to Szczebrzeszyn, originating on the plateau of bastion no. 5, traversed through the former Zamkowy Square, which was later redesigned into Ordonanshauzowa Street leading directly towards the collegiate bell tower. The route then meandered between the church, the palace buildings, and the Szczebrzeska Gate, approaching the latter from the west. It passed through the niche left after the demolished curtain wall II-III. Functioning as the Szczebrzeszyński Wyjazd, it ran alongside the former guardhouse on the ravelin, merging with the original route on the causeway827.

The dismantling of the fortress created an opportunity to connect the two largest suburbs with the Old Town. The unfavourable regulations that prevented construction within 600 fathoms from the fortress walls were no longer in effect, which benefited the city’s development. However, the property ownership and the reluctance of military authorities, who held the most valuable post-fortress areas, crucial for the city’s proper growth, still hindered the development. Instead of becoming a central district, the area around the Old Town was occupied by vacant land, military training grounds, and barracks. From 1867 onwards, the period of the most remarkable development of Nowa Osada began, the centre of economic activity, trade, services, and craftsmanship. Nowa Osada became competitive with the Old Town by offering greater spatial expansion possibilities, unrestricted investment freedom, and a local market for trade that ensured sales among the surrounding population. In the New Market (Nowy Rynek), masonry buildings and inns were constructed, and existing townhouses were expanded. Besides shops, weekly fairs were held in the square, attracting residents from the Zamość, Biłgoraj, and Tomaszów districts. At the beginning of the 20th century, the animal trade was relocated to this suburb from the Old Town836. From 1916 to 1917, near the New Market, a narrow-gauge railway, pulled by horses, operated to Miączyn and the sugar factory in Nieledwia. The dominant population within Nowa Osada were Jewish. In the years 1866–1872, they erected a masonry synagogue on Jerozolimska Street, replacing the previous wooden one. In Nowa Osada, small-scale industrial plants operated in the food, distillery, and machinery sectors. One of the largest was the steam brewery “Livonia” (founded by Jonas Peretz), which operated since 1903 on Świętojańska Street. A branch of the Agricultural Machinery and Tools Factory of Mieczysław Wolski from Lublin was established on Lwowska Street, in the outskirts of Nowa Osada and Kolonia Podtopole, in 1894. In 1880, near the relic segment of the Hrubieszów route, Paweł Jabłoński put into use the largest brickyard in Zamość, known as Pawłówka838. This facility had a railway platform on the line to Włodzimierz. Near to it was a wooden windmill, also owned by Jabłoński. An Eastern Orthodox cemetery was situated on the northern edge of Nowa Osada and Kolonia Podtopole. Within this cemetery, in the third quarter of the 19th c., a wooden chapel was built, which was subsequently replaced by a new one in 1910. During World War I, the Germans repurposed the place into a military cemetery839. To the east of the Eastern Orthodox cemetery there was a Muslim cemetery dating back to the 17th c.840 In the plots of Kolonia Podtopole and Szerokadla, the Jewish community established a new cemetery in 1907, replacing the 16th-c. cemetery on Lwowska Street. Apart from the New Market and Lwowska Street, the road network of Nowa Osada encompassed 19 streets, including a route leading towards Hrubieszów841. The urban architecture of Nowa Osada resembled that of provincial towns. In 1886, there were 34 plots in the New Market, of which 28 were developed. The entire suburb had 479 properties, with 215 houses totalling 1,088 rooms. Aside from the New Market, the most densely populated streets were Długa with 31 buildings, Targowisko – 28, and Jerozolimska – 27842. In 1914, the suburb had 244 buildings, including two damaged during wartime. The New Market still had several old arcade-style buildings843. Among the wooden constructions there were cottages and suburban houses, including elite manor-style buildings. In 1866, Nowa Osada had 2,278 residents, surpassing other settlements. By 1904, the suburb consisted of 229 buildings and 4,935 residents. The population consisted of Jews (72.4%), Catholics (23%), and Eastern Orthodox (4.6%). In 1907, the suburb’s population increased to 5,687; in 1911, there were 5,801 residents – 262 more than in the Old Town. The dominant community was Jewish (78.7%),

In contrast to Nowa Osada, the spatial development of the Lubelskie Suburb – Majdanek – was limited due to unfavourable terrain conditions on the eastern side of the Lublin route. The construction mainly concentrated along the road leading to Majdan and a few cross streets. In 1874, there were 55 buildings in the area, but by 1896, this number had decreased to 47. After 1900, three development clusters became prominent: one around the Lublin route with Obwodowa Street junction and two settlements along the eastern side of the northern stretch of the route. The Lubelskie Suburb had a predominantly agricultural character856. The situation changed when several significant industrial facilities developed in the city.In 1883, the Ministry of Communication established a road clinker brickyard on the border between the Lubelskie Suburb and Janowice Małe, along Obwodowa Street. It was the first such brickyard in Polish territories, inspired by a similar facility in Munich. It was the largest workplace in Zamość, employing between 40 to 150 workers. The brickyard used a gas-fired ten-chamber Mandheim kiln and a steam engine with a capacity of 24 hp.857 By the end of the 19th c., most of the city’s streets were paved with clinker, a remarkable development for the Kingdom of Poland. Other facilities were established in 1886 next to the brickyard: the St. Nicholas municipal hospital, a chapel, and a pharmacy858. Furthermore, near the brickyard, the Ministry of Communication constructed (in 1901) a road maintenance depot. Its purpose was to oversee the construction of the first-class national road from Warsaw to Tomaszów. After the departure of the Russian authorities from Zamość, the road supervision function was discontinued, and the depot became a residential building under the management of the clinker brickyard859. Three cemeteries existed on Obwodowa Street: a parish cemetery with a chapel (constructed in the years 1917–1918) funded by Józef Czernicki; a military cemetery established by the Austrian authorities during World War I; and an Eastern Orthodox cemetery, which was closed in 1904 and intersected by a railway line in 1916. The Roman Catholic cemetery was situated next to the Józef Czernicki’s brickyard860. In the 1890s, Andrzej Dziuba established a clinker brickyard on the opposite side of the place861.

The most significant investment in the Lubelskie Suburb was the construction of Russian barracks. Strategically located Zamość gathered significant military forces essential for defensive actions in the early stages of a potential armed conflict. In the summer of 1905, by a compulsory purchase order, the military gained agricultural land covering over 45 hectares for the new barracks. The construction of the military complex took place from 1907 to 1910. As a result, 80 architecturally consistent buildings were erected864. Next to the barracks, a garrison Orthodox Church of the Transfiguration of the Lord (or the Holy Trinity) was constructed in 1908, commonly referred to as the cerkiew spaska or cerkiew butyrska, named after the 66th Infantry Regiment stationed there. After the departure of the Russian authorities from Zamość, the barracks were occupied by the Austro-Hungarian army, which consisted of nearly 1,200 soldiers. Eight buildings were constructed during this period. Additionally, two hospitals with a pharmacy and a laboratory were set up. A military cemetery was established near the closed Orthodox church. From 1915 to 1916, there was a station for the narrow-gauge railway line from Bełżec to Trawniki and a system of railway sidings in operation within the barracks. Starting in 1916, a standard-gauge railway siding was also connected to the military complex.

Zieliński, Zamość w latach 1914–1918 (as n. 614), p. 41, tab. 7. 869 Studium historyczno-urbanistyczne przedmieść (as n. 702), After Poland regained independence, the spatial structure of Zamość began to crystallise due to efforts made between 1916 and 1920 to enlarge and regulate the city’s area. After establishing Zamość boundaries in 1923, the city consisted of the Old Town (Śródmieście or City Centre), Nowa Osada, Lubelskie Suburb, Majdan, Janowice Duże, and Szczebrzeskie Suburb. Over the interwar period, the city’s boundaries were defined, with villages and estates gradually being incorporated. During this period, Zamość experienced dynamic growth as a regional administrative, service, and economic centre. Investments were most intensive in the two largest districts, Nowa Osada and Lubelskie Suburb, where new residential, service, and industrial buildings were constructed. The city’s transport network was modernised and expanded along the roads leading to Lublin, Lviv, Szczebrzeszyn, Hrubieszów, Krasnobród, and Skierbieszów. Between 1934 and 1935, the Karolówka Grange and Błonie, with the Janowice Małe Grange, were annexed to Zamość, creating additional residential and service spaces on the western side of the city870.

During the interwar period, far-reaching plans aimed to elevate Zamość to an important multifunctional city in central Poland. It was necessary to patch up the economic backwardness in relation to other parts of the country, driven by socioeconomic, military, and political factors. The strategy was to invest in Zamość and its region. Thanks to its central location, Zamość was envisioned as a major transportation hub, with crucial railway routes running north-south between Gdańsk and Odesa as well as Lviv and the Gulf of Finland, along with eastwest connections between the Silesian District and Volhynia. The region was intended to be crossed by the A1 motorway, connecting Gdańsk and Gdynia with Lviv and Black Sea ports, as well as an arterial road from the Świętokrzyskie Industrial Region through Sandomierz, Włodzimierz, to Kyiv. Reforms in the country’s administrative structure included making Zamość the centre of the voivodeship. Additionally, the Central Industrial District project aimed to transform the Zamość region into its supply area, focusing on food and light industries. These ambitious plans could not be realised due to the outbreak of World War II871. Zamość held significance as a hub for economic, cultural, and service activities for the surrounding districts within the Zamość region, including Zamość, Tomaszów, Biłgoraj, Hrubieszów, and Krasnystaw. The city was home to institutions of provincial importance, such as a district court with a prosecutor’s office, administrative institutions, and educational facilities. In the spatial structure of Zamość, the centrally located Old Town covered an area of 530 hectares and comprised 230 mostly masonry buildings. By 1919, it was inhabited by approximately 8,000 people, including 5,574 Jews and 3 Eastern Orthodox. The number of permanent residents decreased due to the expansion of the suburbs. By 1935, there were 7,620 registered residents in the Old Town872, and just before the outbreak of World War II, the number had decreased to 4,858. In the Old Town and 870 B. Nowak, J. The 1936–1939 conservation works on the buildings surrounding the market resulted in renovation of the tenements and the city hall. The Salt Market served as the Old Town’s most dominant trade and service centre. Its space was occupied by stalls and rows of kiosks selling various goods and food products. Consequently, the military relinquished control over the church to municipal authorities in 1921. During World War II, the German authorities closed many institutions or reorganised their functions. Several civil structures were repurposed for industrial and storage uses. For instance, the Old Town synagogue was converted into a stable and later into a large carpentry workshop, which led to the deterioration of the state of the building. In 1941, the collegiate church was reorganised to a grain and equipment storage facilities. The post-fortress buildings were utilised as garages, military storage, and supply facilities891. Additionally, numerous street and square names in the city were changed. As part of the preparations for the invasion of the Soviet Union (Operation “Otto”), German authorities modernised the railway infrastructure in 1940. They expanded the technical section of the Zamość station with several additional tracks and the New Osada loading yard. In 1942, a brick railway depot with an administrative building was constructed at the station, along with road management buildings on Szczebrzeska Street. After 1945, Zamość underwent significant social and ownership changes, especially within the city centre. The former Jewish-owned tenements in the Old Town had new residents. Many buildings were neglected, which created a negative image of the Old Town. Due to renovation and conservation efforts carried out in the 1970s and after 2005, the proportion of residential space was gradually reduced in favour of service activities. Despite these efforts, it was impossible to eliminate municipal housing, which were still mainly occupied by lowincome residents of the social margins. In 1996, the Old Town was inhabited by 1,754 people. In the post-war period, Zamość developed by the principles of the socialist economy, serving as the capital of the Zamość region. It became the local centre of administration, service, and economy. Centrally planned investments primarily focused on the manufacturing industry, which employed the local popu- 890 The northeast bypass was included in the project of the spatial development plan of Zamość from 1939 by Jan Zachwatowicz and Władysław Wieczorkiewicz. This industrial zone, created during the interwar period, was concentrated in the city’s eastern part, along the railway line to Hrubieszów. After 1950, the area consisted of enterprises such as large meat processing plants, a cold store, a granary, a construction combine, a furniture factory, a dairy cooperative, housing factory (the facilities producing elements necessary for the construction of prefabricated, concrete residential houses using the “large-panel” technology) as well as numerous processing and storage facilities. Thanks to the population growth, the number of construction investments increased. New residential neighbourhoods emerged, including Podgroble, Zamczysko, Promyk, Wiśniowa, Karolówka, Powiatowa, mainly with single-family housing, and Ludowego Wojska Polskiego, Planty, and Orzeszkowej, with multi-family housing. As part of the national economic development planning trends in the 1960s, urban development projects for the city centre and eastern residential districts emerged, including “Centrum Usług Ogólnomiejskich” (Eng: citywide service centre), “Dzielnica Wschód” (Eng: east district), and “Nowy Zamość” (Eng: new Zamość). These projects were associated with plans to elevate Zamość to the status of the voivodeship capital and industrialise the city. Many of the transportation infrastructure projects proposed during this period were implemented in subsequent decades892. In 1974, the village of Sitaniec-Błonie was incorporated into Zamość, and a part of the unused land was transferred to the Zamość municipality.

After the war, the buildings in Old Town quarters required substantial financial investments due to their tragic condition. In 1957, the green areas at the Mickiewicza Square were modernised; flowerbeds, pathways, and leisure areas were added. The Mickiewicza Square became, alongside the City Park, one of the most popular recreational spots for the Zamość residents and an increasing number of tourists893. The Salt Market lost its status as a trade centre to the New Market and the municipal marketplace on Bazyliańska Street. The degradation of the Water Market as a public square was also noticeable. In the 1960s, the first post-war renovation efforts within the Old Town began. The works included the “Podkarpie” building and the eastern blocks of the Old Town. The former Poor Clares’ convent complex housed the Citizens’ Militia (MO) headquarters and later an orphanage. There was also a notable expansion in tourist infrastructure. Tourist accommodations were mostly centred around the hotels “Centralny” and Staromiejski” (located near Szczebrzeska Gate), as well as the excursion house of the Polish Tourist and Sightseeing Society, which was located in the former kahal building. A modern hotel called “Renesans” was constructed at 6 Grecka Street between 1967 and 1971. In the early 1970s, several railway sidings were dismantled within the Old Town area.Under the law of 28 May 1975896, a two-tier was administrative division was introduced. As a result, Zamość was granted the status of a voivodeship city. In 1974, the city received central funds to revitalise the Old Town in 1975–1985. During this period, Zamość experienced dynamic growth, with plans to expand an area of over 54 square kilometres and increase the population to 100,000–120,000 by 2000. However, the city’s development did not go as fast as anticipated due to political and economic crises.

In terms of housing investments and spatial development, multi-family housing estates were established, including Orzeszkowej, Kilińskiego, Wiejska, Słoneczny Stok, and a complex to three housing estates called “Nowe Miasto”, featuring the nationally exemplary residential estate unit “PR-5” (government program no. 5). Additionally, smaller housing estates were situated in various parts of the city. Single-family housing development continued in neighbourhoods such as Karolówka, Rataja, Nowe Miasto, and Janowice Duże. In 1989, Zamość was divided into residential estates, eliminating the traditional district divisions (including Lubelskie Suburb, Podtopole, and Janowice Małe). The city’s transport network was modernised by creating dual carriageways and constructing two inner-city bypasses897. During the revitalisation of the Old Town, green spaces on the Great Market were removed. In 1980, the surface of the Market was modernised according to the design by Wiktor Zin, and facade lighting was installed on tenements and public buildings. The Great Market became a representative public space. In 1992, the city’s Old Town was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List alongside Cracow and Warsaw. The Salt Market, measuring 90 × 50 metres, underwent a detailed modernisation, gaining a new compositional and spatial dimension. The former military bathhouse and a storage building were demolished, opening the Market towards the west. After the reconstruction, functional zones – for leisure and infrastructure – were marked within it. A new surface, designated flowerbeds and relaxation areas were laid out in the Water Market in 2010. Renovating the former Poor Clares’ convent building, which now houses the State Music School, made the Market more peaceful than the bustling Great Market and Salt Market. In 1992, Pope John Paul II elevated the collegiate church to the rank of a Cathedral for the newly established Roman Catholic Diocese of Zamość-Lubaczów. Between 2010 and 2012, a reconstruction of the church’s historical structure was carried out. The restoration efforts encompassed the high roof, eastern facade, a ridge turret, portico in front of the western entrance, and the bell tower. After 1989, the accommodation infrastructure in Zamość experienced significant development. Seven hotels, guesthouses, and tourist lodgings has been operating in the Old Town. Additionally, several hotels were built in other housing estates. In 1975, the bus station was relocated from the Old Town to New Town. Towards the end of the 1970s, there were plans to close the railway line passing through the city centre and redirect it to the northern railway bypass along the Metallurgy-Sulphur Line (Linia Hutniczo-Siarkowa – LHS)898. The primary goal was to revitalise the Old Town within the boundaries of the 19th-c. fortifications. This initiative gained more interest after 1992 when the Old Town was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List. However, the railway authorities opposed the changes, especially since the railway was an essential component of longdistance transportation. After 2000, there was a decline in railway connections to Zamość, leading to the closure of transport infrastructure. In 2009, railway connections were suspended but restored again in March 2011. Hwilken Hans konigl May Konung Carl den XII. med. das Armeé förby passerade den 22 Sept. 1704 och Campera de wöd Mokre 1-4 mihl ifran Staden, Sedan samma Ort, Sigh Hans Kongl May: submitterat hade och säledes för fienteligit anfall befriat Podziałka liniowa wyrażona w sążniach szwedzkich, skala ok. 1: 4000, orientacja południowa (S), wymiary 39,5 × 34 cm. Plan sporządzili szwedzcy inżynierowie wojskowi podczas przemarszu króla Karola XII, który 22 września 1704 r. obozował we wsi Mokre. Na planie przedstawiono schematyczny plan miasta i jego fortyfikacji, przekrój fortyfikacji, a także widok Zamościa od strony północno-wschodniej (na oś bastionu VI). Ważniejsze obiekty oznaczono cyframi i objaśniono na kartuszu pod tytułem mapy (1 – kościół farny [kolegiata], 2 – kościół Franciszkanów, 3 – kościół ormiański, 4 – klasztor żeński [klaryski], 5 – synagoga, 6 – cerkiew ruska [greckokatolicka], 7 – ratusz, 8 – Akademia, 9 – zamek [pałac], 10 – numer naniesiono na plan i do legendy, ale nie objaśniono, oznaczono nim Akademię Zamoyską). Poza dokładnie oznaczonymi fortyfikacjami nie ma zabudowy, która została spalona, podpisano tylko bagno (Morast). Oryg.: Riksarkivet Stokholm, Kartong, nr 41, lit. a. 1.4. zamość, 2nd half of the 17th c. Plan de la Forteresse de Zamosc Author Jan Michał Link, unmarked scale, about 1:4000, dimensions 15.5 × 24 cm, etching in the book F. G. de Jonsaca, Histoire de Stanislas Jablonowski castellan de Cracvie grand general des armees de Pologne, Leipzig 1774, p. 24. The map presents the street grid and outlines of important buildings, as well as details of fortifications. Sixteen key objects are marked with letters, which are described in the legend in French as follows (A – castle, B – parish church [collegiate church], C – academy, D – Great Market, E – Water Market, F – Salt Market, G – town hall, H – Franciscan convent (incorrectly labelled as Capuchin), I – Franciscan church, K – Brothers Hospitallers’ church, L – Armenian church, M – Greek Catholic church (incorrectly marked in place of the synagogue), N – synagogue (incorrectly marked in the Armenian cemetery), O – Lwowska Gate, P – Lubelska Gate, Q – mill). Zamojsc. Hwilken Hans konigl May Konung Carl den XII. med. das Armeé förby passerade den 22 Sept. 1704 och Campera de wöd Mokre 1–4 mihl ifran Staden, Sedan samma Ort, Sigh Hans Kongl May: submitterat hade och säledes för fienteligit anfall befriat Linear scale expressed in Swedish fathoms, scale about 1:4000, oriented south (S), dimensions 39.5 × 34 cm. The map was drawn by Swedish military engineers during the march of King Charles XII, who camped in the village of Mokre on 22 September 1704. The map depicts a schematic layout of the city and its fortifications, a cross-section of the fortifications, and a view of Zamość from the northeast (on the axis of bastion VI). Major objects are marked with numbers and explained in a cartouche under the map title (1 – parish church [collegiate church], 2 – Franciscan church, 3 – Armenian church, 4 – women’s monastery [Poor Clares], 5 – synagogue, 6 – Ruthenian church [Greek Catholic], 7 – town hall, 8 – Academy, 9 – castle [palace], no. 10 – included on the plan and in the legend, but not explained, denoting the Zamoyski Academy). Apart from the precisely marked fortifications, there are no buildings left standing; only the marsh (Morast) is labelled.

Additionally, map illustrates important roads outside the city, suburbs, and the terrain relief. Orig.: Staatsarchiv in Wien, Kriegsarchiv, GLK 159. Publ.: Kartograficzne Zamosciana, p. 115. The map marks 21 key objects with numerical signatures, which are explained in the legend as follows (1 – parish church [collegiate church], 2 – Franciscan nunnery [Poor Clares], 3 – Basilian monastery, 4 – Reformed Franciscan monastery, 5 – Brothers Hospitallers’ monastery, 6 – Armenian church, 7 – Franciscan monastery, 8 – Academy, 9 – Theological seminary and clergy residences [Thomhern Wohnungen], 10 – castle, 11 – city hall, 12 – Jewish school, 13 – fire-ravaged areas [blocks of buildings between today’s Żeromskiego, Kolegiacka, Moranda streets and curtain IIIII], 14 – Lubelska Gate, 15 – bakery, 16 – powder magazine, 17 –Lwowska Gate, 18 – Szczebrzeska Gate, 19 – arsenal, 20 – passages in side flanks, 21 – passages in the bricked-up flanks [walls]).

Orig. Österreichisches Staatsarchiv in Wien, Kriegsarchiv, ref. no. Glk 159-3. Publ.: Kartograficzne Zamosciana, p. 116. Plan de Zamosc Author Gomez de Parientos, manuscript multicoloured on cardboard, dimensions 33 × 43 cm, linear scale expressed in paces, unmarked scale – about 1: 3600, oriented north, north east (NNE) The more important objects are marked with letters, explained in the top right corner of the map (A – castle, B – city hall, C – arsenal, D – Lwowska Gate, E – Szczebrzeska Gate, F – blind gate [Janowicka], G – parish church [collegiate church], H – Franciscan monastery and church, J – church and monastery of Friars Minor, K – Basilians, L – Brothers Hospitallers, M – Armenian church, N – nunnery [Poor Clares], O – Latin school named Academy, P – suburbs with a width of 700-800 paces). The map depicts the layout of the suburbs, road and water network, terrain relief, and gardens. Buildings of religious significance such as churches, chapels, and synagogues are marked in a darker shade of red. Orig. Österreichisches Staatsarchiv in Wien, Kriegsarchiv, ref. no. Glk 160. Publ.: Kartograficzne Zamosciana, p. 119. Plan von Neu Zamosze in Keyserl[ichen] Pohlen Author Michael Kandlbinder, manuscript, multicoloured on cardboard, dimensions 45.8 × 65.5 cm, no scale bar, unmarked scale – about 1:1700, oriented north. Made as a copy of map no. 8 (1777). The map depicts the city within the fortifications, including the network of streets and places, green areas, and outlines of some buildings. Objects of religious function, including the synagogue, are highlighted with a darker colour [excluding demolished churches, the Franciscan monasteries and Poor Clares]. Orig. Österreichisches Staatsarchiv in Wien, Kriegsarchiv, ref. no. Glk 159-3. Publ.: Kartograficzne Zamosciana, p. 120. Plan von der Festung Zamosc nebst herum liegenden Situation Author Jean de Grüss, manuscript, multicoloured on cardboard, dimensions 47 × 60 cm, linear scale expressed in paces, unmarked scale – about 1:7900, oriented north, north east (NNW). On the map, important city landmarks are marked with letters, which are explained in the upper right corner (A – castle, B – parish church [collegiate church], C – Reformed Franciscan church, D – Armenian church, E – Brothers Hospitallers’ church, F – Franciscan church, G – nunnery [Sisters of Mercy], H – Basilian monastery, I – arsenal, K – Lwowska Gate, L – Szczebrzeska Gate, M – blind gate [Janowicka], N – main guardhouse, O – bakery [Bekerey, kurtyna]). On the map, the main roads leading out of the city are labelled, including the postal road from Lublin to Lviv, brickworks, some suburbs, and villages (Podkrobie [Podgroble], Zadowisko [Sadowisko], Janowitz [Janowice], Wólki [Wólka Miejska]). The terrain relief is marked, including wetlands and ponds. Orig. Österreichisches Staatsarchiv in Wien, Kriegsarchiv, ref. no. Glk 161. Publ.: Kartograficzne Zamosciana, p. 145.

Plan de la Prose d’assaut de la place Zamość, dans la nuit du 19 au 20 mai 1809 par les troupes Polonaises Author Marcin Ciołkowski, manuscript, multicoloured on cardboard, dimensions 55 × 40.5 cm, unmarked scale – about 1: 6000, oriented south. The map depicts the siege of the city by Polish forces. Individual units are marked with letter signatures and explained in the legend. The map presents details of suburban development, road network, gardens, physiography, and wetlands. Orig. Archiwum Narodowe w Krakowie, Zbiory kartograficzne, ref. no. VI 293, p. 18. Publ.: Kartograficzne Zamosciana, p. 125. Plan de la Place de Zamość pour servir au Rapport de 1 Mai 1817 sur la Situation de la Place Authors General Jean Baptiste Malletski and General Jan Paweł Lelewel, manuscript, multicoloured on cardboard, dimensions 68.5 × 52.1 cm, linear scale expressed in fathoms and arshins (yards), unmarked scale – about 1: 2300, oriented north, north east (NNE). The map, prepared in French, was created as documentation for the modernization of the fortress. The bastions are numbered, while public utility buildings and religious buildings occupied by the military are marked with letter signatures. The map shows major roads, wetlands, and defensive installations of the outer belt of the fortress fortifications. Orig. AGAD, Zbiór kartograficzny, ref. no. 94-2. Publ.: Kartograficzne Zamosciana, p. 133. Plan général des Travaux de Fortification éxécuté dans la Place de Zamość pendant la Campagne de 1823 Unknown author, manuscript, multicoloured on cardboard, dimensions 30.6 × 24.9 cm, linear scale expressed in fathoms, unmarked scale – about 1: 6500, oriented north, north east (NNE). The map documents the construction work carried out on the fortress in 1823. Existing roads in the fortress’s forecourt, as well as the bypass road and other planned roads, city gates, and numbered bastions, are labelled. Blocks of buildings in the city are marked, with properties occupied by the army highlighted with blue. Orig. Wojewódzka Biblioteka Publiczna im. Hieronima łopacińskiego w Lublinie, ref. no. 30. Publ.: Kartograficzne Zamosciana, p. 143. Plan des Projekts des Fortification sur la place de Zamość Author Jean Baptiste Malletski and lejtn. Linda, manuscript, multicoloured on paper, dimensions 91.5 × 85.7 cm, 3 linear scales expressed in fathoms, unmarked scale – about 1:1800, oriented north, north east (NNE). This is an addition to map no. 13. It includes an inventory of the defensive works in the fortress, marked with letter signatures and explained in the legend. Blocks of buildings in the city are marked, distinguishing military, religious, and private properties, with street names added. Green areas, gardens, and wells are highlighted. The layout of the bypass roads and the distribution of garrison gardens are marked in the fortress’s forecourt. Orig. AGAD, Zbiór kartograficzny, ref. no. 383-2. Publ.: Kartograficzne Zamosciana, p. 148.

Generalnyj płan krepostii Zamoscja s okrestnostiami na dve vërsty Author Kuźmin, second-class conductor, approved by lieut. Robert von Nolte, manuscript, multicoloured dimensions 51.3 × 47.3 cm, linear scale expressed in Russian fathoms, unmarked scale – about 1: 8400, oriented north. The map depicts the fortress and its surroundings within a radius of 2 versts. Military objects are marked in blue, religious buildings are labelled. Main roads leading out of the city, settlements, cemeteries, and important landmarks are labelled. Orig. Zakład Architektury Polskiej Politechniki Warszawskiej, U II 65. Publ.: Kartograficzne Zamosciana, p. 160. Sytuacjonnyj płan goroda Zamostias pokazaniem predpo łogajemoj Zamienny uczastkow pod postrojku Jewrejskoj Bolnicy na 20 krawatiej Author unknown, manuscript, multicoloured on paper, dimensions 56 × 66 cm, traverse scale expressed in Russian fathoms, unmarked scale – about 1:4100, oriented north west (NW). The map, prepared in connection with the planned construction of a Jewish hospital with 20 beds, depicts the area of the Old Town and fragments of suburban buildings located on the northern and eastern sides of the city. Different colours are used to distinguish between brick and wooden buildings, as well as the surface of roadways. Orig. Archiwum Państwowe w Zamościu, Akta miasta Zamościa 1821–1915, ref. no. 316, p. 91. Publ.: Kartograficzne Zamosciana, p. 171. Manuscript, multicoloured on paper, dimensions 67.2 × 84.5, scale – about 1:10,000. The map was prepared for official purposes and depicts the distribution of the population within the structural units of the city. It includes a street grid, railway line, cemeteries, population zones based on the number of people residing per 1 hectare, green areas, and a reserve area for residential development. Orig. Archiwum Państwowe w Zamościu, Akta miasta Zamościa 1915–1939, ref. no. 650. Publ.: Kartograficzne Zamosciana, p. 181. 1.18. zamość. Spatial development map, 1939 Zamość. Szkicowy projekt planu zabudowania Authors Jan Zachwatowicz and Władysław Wieczorkiewicz, dimensions 60 × 47 cm, scale 1:10,000. The synthetic map encompasses the results of multi-year studies on the spatial development of the city. The map includes zones of planned development, the proposed street grid, and the boundary of the historic urban complex. What is visible on the map is the concept of changing the city’s structure into a dual-centred one, with centres in the Old and New Towns forming a central hub. Orig. Archiwum Państwowe w Zamościu, Biuro Planowania Prze strzennego w Zamościu, Spis zdawczo-odbiorczy no. 5, lp. 54. Publ.: Kartograficzne Zamosciana, p. 182.

Zamość. Odrys planu ogólnego Author arch. [unknown name] Młynarczyk, dimensions 44.5 × 60.4 cm, scale 1:10,000. The map depicts the city within its administrative boundaries, highlighting the historic centre, the boundary of the protected zone of the Old Town and enlarged industrial zone, indicating changes to the transportation layout in the eastern part of the city. Orig. Archiwum Państwowe w Zamościu, Biuro Planowania Prze strzennego w Zamościu, Spis zdawczo-odbiorczy no. 5, lp. 59. Publ.: Kartograficzne Zamosciana, p. 187. The topographic map, in a scale of 1:10,000, was prepared as a multi-coloured printed publication based on the coordinate system ‘1992’ with the Kronsztad 86 vertical datum. The area of Zamość covers five sheets, each measuring 59 × 60 cm. The thematic scope includes physiography and anthropogenic elements (such as property structure, functional classification of buildings, road network, green areas, and administrative boundaries). 2. Zamoscium. Nova Poloniae civitas a magnifico eius Regni Cancellario a fundamentis extructa Hand-coloured copperplate engraving, engraver F. de Vit Amstelodoni, dimensions 46 × 35 cm. Oldest view of the city, axonometric view, oriented south. This view depicts the city within its walls with 8 bastions, surrounded by a moat. Important buildings within the city are marked with letter signatures. The spatial perspective of the city has been distorted to show the entire layout of the buildings.
